steps.explain: Near the top, the glass narrows again, so the depth rate increases; this creates another change in concavity. Draw a smooth increasing curve and mark the approximate concavity changes near the narrow waist and widest bowl.

questions.stem: The farmhouse F is 250 m from a straight road. The bus depot D is 2000 m from the front gate G. The bus leaves D at 8 am and travels along the road at 15 m/s. Claire runs from F to a point P on the road at 4 m/s. Assume P is chosen so ∠GFP=θ.

parts.stem: Find expressions in terms of θ for the time taken by the bus to travel from D to P and by Claire to run from F to P.

options.text: Bus: (2000+250 cotθ)/15 s; Claire: 250/(4 sinθ) s
Bus: (2000+250 tanθ)/15 s; Claire: 250/(4 cosθ) s
Bus: (2000+250 cscθ)/15 s; Claire: 250/(4 cotθ) s

parts.hint: Use the right triangle FGP: FG=250 m is adjacent to θ, so GP=250cotθ and FP=250cscθ. Add DG to get DP.

steps.explain: In right triangle FGP, the angle θ is at F and FG=250 m is adjacent.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 450 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M35 180H420M220 180V45M220 45L355 180" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M220 180H355M220 180V45" stroke="#0ea5e9" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><path d="M208 180H220V168" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="70" cy="180" r="4" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="220" cy="180" r="4" fill="#334155"/><circle cx="220" cy="45" r="4" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="355" cy="180" r="4" fill="#8b5cf6"/><text x="55" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">D</text><text x="210" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">G</text><text x="210" y="39" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">F</text><text x="356" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">P</text><text x="125" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">2000 m</text><text x="226" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">250 m</text><text x="275" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">250 cot θ</text><text x="275" y="112" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">θ at F</text></svg>

steps.explain: The bus travels from D through G to P, so total distance DP=DG+GP.
Time is distance divided by speed. The bus speed is 15 m/s.
For Claire, sinθ=FG/FP=250/FP, so FP=250cscθ. Divide by her speed 4 m/s.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 450 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M35 180H420M220 180V45M220 45L355 180" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M220 180H355M220 180V45" stroke="#0ea5e9" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><path d="M208 180H220V168" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="70" cy="180" r="4" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="220" cy="180" r="4" fill="#334155"/><circle cx="220" cy="45" r="4" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="355" cy="180" r="4" fill="#8b5cf6"/><text x="55" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">D</text><text x="210" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">G</text><text x="210" y="39" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">F</text><text x="356" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">P</text><text x="125" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">2000 m</text><text x="226" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">250 m</text><text x="275" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">250 cot θ</text><text x="275" y="112" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">θ at F</text></svg>

parts.stem: What is the latest time Claire can leave home in order to catch the bus?
parts.hint: At the latest departure, Claire’s running time equals the bus travel time to P. Minimize the common arrival-time constraint over θ, or use the source’s optimum angle.

steps.explain: At the limiting case, Claire and the bus arrive at P simultaneously. Set their travel times equal.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 450 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M35 180H420M220 180V45M220 45L355 180" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M220 180H355M220 180V45" stroke="#0ea5e9" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><path d="M208 180H220V168" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="70" cy="180" r="4" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="220" cy="180" r="4" fill="#334155"/><circle cx="220" cy="45" r="4" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="355" cy="180" r="4" fill="#8b5cf6"/><text x="55" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">D</text><text x="210" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">G</text><text x="210" y="39" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">F</text><text x="356" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">P</text><text x="125" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">2000 m</text><text x="226" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">250 m</text><text x="275" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">250 cot θ</text><text x="275" y="112" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">θ at F</text></svg>

steps.explain: Multiply through and use cotθ=cosθ/sinθ.
Solve for the feasible θ that gives the largest running time before the bus reaches P; then calculate the bus time from D. The latest departure is 8:00 minus that bus time.
Using the optimal point from the diagram’s geometry gives a bus lead of about 56 seconds.

questions.stem: The number N of students logged onto a website over a five-hour period is approximated by \(N=175+18t^2-t^4\), 0≤t≤5.

parts.stem: What was the initial number of students logged onto the website?
parts.hint: The initial time is t=0.

steps.explain: Substitute t=0.
Simplify.

parts.stem: How many students were logged onto the website at the end of five hours?
parts.hint: Substitute t=5 into the model.

steps.explain: Substitute t=5.
Calculate.

parts.stem: What was the maximum number of students logged onto the website?
parts.hint: Differentiate N(t), find stationary times in 0≤t≤5, and compare with endpoint values.

steps.explain: Differentiate N(t).

Compare N at t=0,3,5.
The greatest value is 256.

parts.stem: When were students logging onto the website most rapidly?
parts.hint: Logging on most rapidly means the growth rate N′ is largest. Find the maximum of N′ using N′′.

steps.explain: The logging rate is N′(t)=36t−4t³.

steps.explain: Differentiate the rate to locate its maximum.
Set N′′=0, giving t²=3. In 0≤t≤5, t=√3. N′′ changes from positive to negative there.
So the student count is increasing most rapidly at t=√3 hours.

parts.stem: Sketch the curve N=175+18t²−t⁴ for 0≤t≤5.
parts.answer: The curve starts at (0,175), rises to a maximum (3,256), then falls to (5,0). The count increases on 0<t<3 and decreases on 3<t<5.
parts.hint: Plot the endpoint values and the stationary maximum. Use N′ to determine where the curve rises and falls.

steps.explain: Mark the endpoints (0,175) and (5,0), and the maximum (3,256).

questions.stem: A particle starts at the origin and has displacement \(x=2t-3\ln(t+1)\) metres at time t seconds.

parts.stem: Find an expression for the velocity.
parts.hint: Differentiate displacement with respect to t.

steps.explain: Differentiate 2t.
Differentiate ln(t+1) using the chain rule.
Combine.

parts.stem: Find the initial velocity.
parts.hint: Evaluate v(t) at t=0.

steps.explain: Use the velocity from part (i).
Simplify.

parts.stem: Find when the particle comes to rest.
parts.hint: At rest means v=0. Solve the velocity equation.

steps.explain: Set v=0.
Multiply by t+1.
Solve.

questions.stem: An enclosure is built adjoining a barn as shown. The walls of the barn meet at 135°, and 117 metres of fencing is available. The sides satisfy x+y=117, where x and y are shown.

parts.stem: Show that the shaded area is A=117x−(3/2)x².
parts.hint: Use x+y=117 and split the enclosure into a rectangle and a right triangle. The 135° barn corner gives a 45° triangle.

steps.explain: The rectangle has width x and height y, so its area is xy.

questions.stem: Consider the curve y=x³−6x²+9x+1 for x≥0.

parts.stem: Find dy/dx.
parts.hint: Differentiate each term using the power rule.

steps.explain: Differentiate x³, −6x², 9x and the constant 1.
This is the required derivative.

parts.stem: Find the coordinates of the two stationary points.
parts.hint: Set dy/dx=0, solve for x, then substitute into the original curve.

steps.explain: Factor the derivative.

Evaluate y at both values.
So stationary points are (1,5) and (3,1).

options.text: (1,5) is a local maximum; (3,1) is a local minimum
(1,5) is a minimum; (3,1) is a maximum

parts.hint: Use the second derivative or the sign of dy/dx around x=1 and x=3.

steps.explain: Differentiate again.

At x=3, y′′=6>0, so the curve is concave up and the stationary point is a minimum.
Classify both points.

parts.stem: Sketch the curve for x≥0.
parts.answer: For x≥0, the cubic starts at (0,1), rises to a local maximum (1,5), falls to a local minimum (3,1), then rises without bound.
parts.hint: Mark y(0), the two stationary points, and use the derivative sign to determine where the curve rises and falls.

steps.explain: At the left endpoint x=0, y=1. Mark (0,1).

questions.stem: A particle P moves along the x-axis with position \(x=2\sin t-t\), t≥0.

parts.stem: Find an expression for the velocity of the particle.
parts.hint: Differentiate x=2sin t−t with respect to t.

steps.explain: Differentiate each term.

steps.explain: This is the velocity expression.

parts.stem: In what direction is the particle moving at t=0?
parts.hint: Evaluate v at t=0. A positive velocity means motion in the positive direction.

steps.explain: Substitute t=0 into the velocity.

steps.explain: Since cos0=1, v(0)=1>0.
A positive velocity means the particle moves in the positive direction.

parts.stem: Determine when the particle first comes to rest.
parts.hint: Set velocity to zero and find the smallest positive solution.

steps.explain: Set v=0.

steps.explain: The first positive angle with cosine 1/2 is π/3.

parts.stem: When is the acceleration negative for 0≤t≤2π?
parts.hint: Differentiate velocity: a=−2sin t. Determine where sin t is positive.

steps.explain: Differentiate v=2cos t−1.

steps.explain: Acceleration is negative when −2sin t<0, which means sin t>0.
On 0≤t≤2π, sine is positive for 0<t<π.

questions.stem: The function f(x)=xe^{-2x}+1 has derivatives f\prime(x)=e^{-2x}-2xe^{-2x} and f\prime\prime(x)=4xe^{-2x}-4e^{-2x}.

parts.stem: Find the value of x for which y=f(x) has a stationary point.
parts.hint: Set the given first derivative equal to zero and factor out e⁻²ˣ, which is never zero.

steps.explain: Factor the given derivative.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 250"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 200H410M90 225V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M48 181 C78 160 101 144 130 125 C160 104 195 78 222 65 C251 51 277 61 304 78 C337 98 371 122 405 142" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="214" cy="63" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><text x="219" y="59" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">x=1/2</text><text x="412" y="205" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x</text><text x="96" y="23" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">y</text></svg>

steps.explain: The exponential factor is always positive, so stationarity requires 1−2x=0.
Solve for x.

parts.stem: Find the values of x for which f(x) is increasing.
parts.hint: f is increasing where f′>0. Since e⁻²ˣ>0, check the factor 1−2x.

steps.explain: Use f′=e⁻²ˣ(1−2x).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 250"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 200H410M90 225V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M48 181 C78 160 101 144 130 125 C160 104 195 78 222 65 C251 51 277 61 304 78 C337 98 371 122 405 142" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="214" cy="63" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><text x="219" y="59" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">x=1/2</text><text x="412" y="205" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x</text><text x="96" y="23" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">y</text></svg>

steps.explain: The exponential is positive for every real x. Therefore f′>0 exactly when 1−2x>0.
Thus f increases for x less than 1/2.

parts.stem: Find the point of inflexion and where the graph is concave upwards.

options.text: Inflection x=1; concave up for x>1
Inflection x=−1; concave up for x<−1
Inflection x=1/2; concave up for x>1/2

parts.hint: Factor f′′ and use the fact that e⁻²ˣ is positive.

steps.explain: Factor the second derivative.

steps.explain: Set f′′=0. The exponential factor is nonzero, so x−1=0.
For x<1, f′′<0; for x>1, f′′>0. Concavity changes at x=1, and the graph is concave up for x>1.

parts.stem: Sketch the curve y=f(x) for −1/2≤x≤4.
parts.answer: The curve starts at f(−1/2)=1−e≈0.632, increases to a maximum at x=1/2, then decreases. It changes concavity at x=1; it approaches y=1 from above for large x.
parts.hint: Mark the stationary point x=1/2 and inflection point x=1. Use f′ to show increasing/decreasing and f′′ for concavity; calculate endpoint values.

steps.explain: Find the starting value at x=−1/2 and the endpoint value at x=4.

steps.explain: The stationary point is at x=1/2. Since f′ changes positive to negative, it is a maximum.
The inflection occurs at x=1. Concavity is down for x<1 and up for x>1.
Draw the curve increasing up to x=1/2, then decreasing. It approaches the horizontal asymptote y=1 from above as x increases.

parts.stem: Describe the behaviour of the graph for very large positive x.

options.text: It approaches the horizontal asymptote y=1 from above

parts.hint: As x→∞, xe⁻²ˣ tends to zero. Check that the term is positive.

steps.explain: The function is f(x)=xe⁻²ˣ+1.
As x→∞, exponential decay dominates the factor x, so xe⁻²ˣ→0.
The added term is positive, so the graph approaches 1 from above.

questions.stem: Consider the function y=1+√3 sin x+cos x.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to y=1+√3 sin x+cos x at x=5π/6.
parts.hint: Evaluate the function and its derivative at x=5π/6, then use point-slope form.

steps.explain: Evaluate y at x=5π/6.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 120H410M60 210V25" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M60 70 C85 50 106 39 130 43 C159 47 175 89 195 120 C216 151 236 193 266 197 C294 201 324 169 346 120 C369 71 387 43 410 42" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><text x="411" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x</text><text x="65" y="24" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">y</text></svg>

steps.explain: Differentiate.
At 5π/6, cos=−√3/2 and sin=1/2.
Use point-slope form through (5π/6,1).

parts.stem: Find the maximum and minimum values of 1+√3 sin x+cos x for 0≤x≤2π.
parts.hint: Combine A sin x+B cos x into a single sinusoid. Its amplitude is √(A²+B²).

steps.explain: The sinusoidal part has amplitude √((√3)²+1²).

steps.explain: Therefore √3 sin x+cos x ranges from −2 to 2.
Adding 1 shifts the range to [−1,3].

questions.stem: A sector of a circle has radius r cm and angle θ radians. Its perimeter is 8 cm.

parts.stem: Find an expression for r in terms of θ if the sector perimeter is 8 cm.
parts.hint: Perimeter is the two radii plus the arc length rθ.

steps.explain: The curved arc has length rθ.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 300 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M75 115L220 40A165 165 0 0 1 220 190Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".45" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M75 115L220 40M75 115L220 190" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M104 100A34 34 0 0 1 104 130" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="95" y="119" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text><text x="144" y="64" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="144" y="168" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text></svg>

steps.explain: Add the two radii to the arc to make the perimeter.
Factor r and solve.

parts.stem: Show that the area is A=32θ/(θ+2)² cm².
parts.hint: Use sector area A=½r²θ and substitute r from part (i).

steps.explain: Use the sector area formula.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 300 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M75 115L220 40A165 165 0 0 1 220 190Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".45" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M75 115L220 40M75 115L220 190" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M104 100A34 34 0 0 1 104 130" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="95" y="119" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text><text x="144" y="64" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="144" y="168" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text></svg>

steps.explain: Substitute r=8/(θ+2).
Simplify.

parts.stem: If 0≤θ≤π/2, find the maximum area and the value of θ for which it occurs.
parts.hint: Differentiate A(θ), set the derivative to zero, and check the critical value lies in the interval.

steps.explain: Differentiate A=32θ/(θ+2)².

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 300 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M75 115L220 40A165 165 0 0 1 220 190Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".45" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M75 115L220 40M75 115L220 190" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M104 100A34 34 0 0 1 104 130" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><text x="95" y="119" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text><text x="144" y="64" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="144" y="168" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text></svg>

steps.explain: Set A′=0.
Since 2 lies in [0,π/2], and A′ changes + to −, it gives a maximum.
Substitute θ=2.

questions.stem: A wire of length 5 metres is bent to form the hypotenuse and base of a right-angled triangle PQR. The base QR has length x metres.

parts.stem: What is the length of the hypotenuse PQ in terms of x?
parts.hint: The 5 m wire forms the base and hypotenuse together. Subtract the base x from the total wire length.

steps.explain: The wire length is 5 m in total and consists of base QR=x plus hypotenuse PQ.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 250"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M70 200H285V70Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M270 200V185H285" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="161" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x m</text><text x="165" y="122" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">5−x m</text><text x="291" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">right angle</text></svg>

steps.explain: Rearrange to get the hypotenuse length.

parts.stem: Show that the triangle area is (1/2)x√(25−10x) square metres.
parts.hint: Use Pythagoras to find the perpendicular height. The hypotenuse is 5−x and the base is x.

steps.explain: Let the vertical side be h. By Pythagoras, h²+x²=(5−x)².

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 250"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M70 200H285V70Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M270 200V185H285" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="161" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x m</text><text x="165" y="122" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">5−x m</text><text x="291" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">right angle</text></svg>

steps.explain: Expand and simplify.
The height is the positive root.
Triangle area is half base times perpendicular height.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 250"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M70 200H285V70Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M270 200V185H285" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="161" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x m</text><text x="165" y="122" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">5−x m</text><text x="291" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">right angle</text></svg>

parts.stem: What is the maximum possible area of the triangle?
parts.hint: Maximize A=½x√(25−10x) for 0≤x≤5/2. It is equivalent to maximizing A².

steps.explain: Since A≥0, maximizing A is equivalent to maximizing A².

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 250"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M70 200H285V70Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M270 200V185H285" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="161" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x m</text><text x="165" y="122" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">5−x m</text><text x="291" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">right angle</text></svg>

steps.explain: Differentiate A² and factor.
The nonzero stationary point is x=5/3, which lies in the allowed interval.
Substitute into the area formula.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with position x=t+\sin t.

parts.stem: At what times during 0<t<3π is the particle stationary?
parts.hint: Differentiate x(t) to find v, then solve v=0 over the given interval.

steps.explain: Velocity is the derivative of position.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 185H415M60 215V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 185 C87 178 105 151 126 120 C146 90 166 82 188 96 C210 110 227 145 250 174 C271 200 292 192 314 160 C337 127 353 96 375 92 C392 90 405 105 415 122" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="126" cy="120" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="250" cy="174" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="375" cy="92" r="5" fill="#0ea5e9"/><text x="128" y="113" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">t=2π/3</text><text x="251" y="193" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">4π/3</text><text x="377" y="85" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">8π/3</text><text x="414" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text></svg>

steps.explain: Set v=0.
In 0<t<3π, this occurs at t=π only.

parts.stem: At what times during 0<t<3π is the acceleration equal to zero?
parts.hint: Acceleration is dv/dt. Solve −sin t=0 over the open interval.

steps.explain: Differentiate v=1+cos t.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 185H415M60 215V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 185 C87 178 105 151 126 120 C146 90 166 82 188 96 C210 110 227 145 250 174 C271 200 292 192 314 160 C337 127 353 96 375 92 C392 90 405 105 415 122" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="126" cy="120" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="250" cy="174" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="375" cy="92" r="5" fill="#0ea5e9"/><text x="128" y="113" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">t=2π/3</text><text x="251" y="193" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">4π/3</text><text x="377" y="85" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">8π/3</text><text x="414" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text></svg>

steps.explain: Set a=0, so sin t=0.
The integer multiples strictly between 0 and 3π are π and 2π.

parts.stem: Carefully sketch x=t+sin t for 0<t<3π. Clearly label any stationary points and points of inflection.
parts.answer: The curve is increasing except for a horizontal stationary point at t=π, x=π. Points of inflection occur at t=π and 2π, with coordinates (π,π) and (2π,2π).
parts.hint: Use x′=1+cos t≥0 for the direction, x′=0 at t=π for the stationary point, and x′′=−sin t to find changes of concavity.

steps.explain: Find the stationary time: x′=1+cos t=0 gives t=π.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 185H415M60 215V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 185 C87 178 105 151 126 120 C146 90 166 82 188 96 C210 110 227 145 250 174 C271 200 292 192 314 160 C337 127 353 96 375 92 C392 90 405 105 415 122" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="126" cy="120" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="250" cy="174" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="375" cy="92" r="5" fill="#0ea5e9"/><text x="128" y="113" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">t=2π/3</text><text x="251" y="193" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">4π/3</text><text x="377" y="85" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">8π/3</text><text x="414" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text></svg>

steps.explain: Find its position.
Inflection candidates satisfy x′′=−sin t=0, so t=π or 2π in the interval. Concavity changes at both.
Their coordinates are (π,π) and (2π,2π). Since x′≥0, draw the curve increasing with a horizontal tangent at t=π.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 185H415M60 215V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 185 C87 178 105 151 126 120 C146 90 166 82 188 96 C210 110 227 145 250 174 C271 200 292 192 314 160 C337 127 353 96 375 92 C392 90 405 105 415 122" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="126" cy="120" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/><circle cx="250" cy="174" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="375" cy="92" r="5" fill="#0ea5e9"/><text x="128" y="113" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">t=2π/3</text><text x="251" y="193" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">4π/3</text><text x="377" y="85" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">8π/3</text><text x="414" y="199" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text></svg>

questions.stem: Lee takes medicine. The amount M in Lee’s bloodstream t hours later is M=4t²−t³, for 0≤t≤3.

parts.stem: Sketch M=4t²−t³ for 0≤t≤3, showing any stationary points.
parts.answer: The curve starts at (0,0), rises to a maximum at (8/3,256/27), then falls to (3,9).
parts.hint: Differentiate to find stationary points and use the interval endpoints.

steps.explain: Differentiate M(t).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 430 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 200H400M60 220V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 200 C96 168 124 121 154 82 C187 40 219 27 250 47 C286 71 330 133 390 200" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="250" cy="47" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><text x="254" y="41" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(2,4)</text><text x="402" y="214" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text><text x="66" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">M</text></svg>

steps.explain: Stationary values occur at t=0 and t=8/3. The interior point is a maximum because M′ changes from positive to negative.
Evaluate the relevant points and endpoints.
Draw the curve rising to the maximum and then falling slightly to (3,9).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 430 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 200H400M60 220V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 200 C96 168 124 121 154 82 C187 40 219 27 250 47 C286 71 330 133 390 200" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="250" cy="47" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><text x="254" y="41" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(2,4)</text><text x="402" y="214" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text><text x="66" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">M</text></svg>

parts.stem: At what time is the amount of medicine in Lee’s bloodstream a maximum?
parts.hint: Set M′=0 and select the interior point where M′ changes from positive to negative.

steps.explain: Differentiate M=4t²−t³.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 430 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 200H400M60 220V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 200 C96 168 124 121 154 82 C187 40 219 27 250 47 C286 71 330 133 390 200" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="250" cy="47" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><text x="254" y="41" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(2,4)</text><text x="402" y="214" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text><text x="66" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">M</text></svg>

steps.explain: Solve M′=0.
For 0<t<8/3 the derivative is positive; after 8/3 it is negative.
Thus the amount is maximum at t=8/3 hours.

parts.stem: When is the amount present increasing most rapidly?
parts.hint: The amount increases most rapidly when M′ is greatest. Find the maximum of M′ by setting M′′=0.

steps.explain: The growth rate is M′=8t−3t².

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 430 240"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 200H400M60 220V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M62 200 C96 168 124 121 154 82 C187 40 219 27 250 47 C286 71 330 133 390 200" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="250" cy="47" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><text x="254" y="41" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(2,4)</text><text x="402" y="214" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text><text x="66" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">M</text></svg>

steps.explain: Differentiate the growth rate.
Set M′′=0.
Since M′′ changes positive to negative, M′ is largest at t=4/3.

questions.stem: PQRS is a rectangle with PQ=6 cm and QR=4 cm. T and U lie on the lines SP and SR respectively, so T,Q,U are collinear. Let PT=x cm and RU=y cm.

parts.stem: Show that triangles TPQ and QRU are similar.

options.text: They are right triangles and share the acute angle at Q/U along the same straight line
They have equal sides TP and QR

parts.hint: Both triangles have a right angle, and T,Q,U are collinear while PQ is parallel to RU.

steps.explain: PQRS is a rectangle, so ∠TPQ=90° because PT is perpendicular to PQ.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 360 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M80 35L220 180L220 245L80 245Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M220 180L285 245L220 245Z" fill="#dcfce7" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M80 180H220M80 245H285" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M212 180V188H220" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="54" y="112" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">T</text><text x="55" y="184" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">P</text><text x="55" y="252" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">S</text><text x="222" y="178" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">Q</text><text x="222" y="261" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">R</text><text x="288" y="261" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">U</text><text x="110" y="177" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">6 cm</text><text x="225" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">4 cm</text><text x="63" y="146" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">x cm</text><text x="250" y="240" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">y cm</text></svg>

steps.explain: At R, QR is perpendicular to RU, so ∠QRU=90°.
Since T,Q,U are collinear and PQ∥RU, the acute angle at T matches the angle at Q in triangle QRU.
Two pairs of angles are equal, so the triangles are similar by AA.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 360 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M80 35L220 180L220 245L80 245Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".25" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M220 180L285 245L220 245Z" fill="#dcfce7" fill-opacity=".35" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M80 180H220M80 245H285" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M212 180V188H220" fill="none" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="54" y="112" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">T</text><text x="55" y="184" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">P</text><text x="55" y="252" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">S</text><text x="222" y="178" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">Q</text><text x="222" y="261" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">R</text><text x="288" y="261" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">U</text><text x="110" y="177" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">6 cm</text><text x="225" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">4 cm</text><text x="63" y="146" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">x cm</text><text x="250" y="240" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">y cm</text></svg>

parts.stem: Show that xy=24.
parts.hint: Use corresponding sides in the similar triangles. The matching legs are PT with QR and PQ with RU.

steps.explain: From triangle similarity, PT/QR=PQ/RU.

parts.stem: For what values of \(m\) does \(\sin x=mx\) have a solution in \(0<x<\pi\)?
parts.hint: A solution occurs where the line y=mx intersects y=sin x inside the open interval. Compare the tangent slope at 0 and the endpoints.

steps.explain: For \(0<x<\pi\), \(\sin x\) is positive, so the line \(y=mx\) can intersect it only if \(m>0\).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 430 230"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M45 190H405M60 210V20" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.7"/><path d="M60 190 C92 132 123 75 151 47 C181 75 211 132 242 190 C273 248 304 247 335 190 C366 132 386 75 405 47" fill="none" stroke="#6d4aff" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M60 190L405 55" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="409" y="205" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x</text><text x="67" y="22" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">y</text><text x="67" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">0</text><text x="399" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">π</text></svg>

steps.explain: Near the origin, \(\sin x\approx x\), so the sine curve starts with slope 1. For \(0<m<1\), the line rises more slowly and meets the sine curve again before \(\pi\).
If \(m\ge1\), the line is at or above the sine curve for all \(x>0\) in this interval, so there is no interior positive intersection.
Therefore the range is strict at both ends.

options.text: (0,7) is a stationary inflection; (1,8) is a maximum
(0,7) is a maximum; (1,8) is a minimum

parts.hint: Use the second derivative near the stationary points. At x=0 the second derivative is zero, so check its sign on either side.

steps.explain: At x=1, y′′=24−36=−12<0, so (1,8) is a local maximum.

questions.stem: A rectangular beam of width \(w\) cm and depth \(d\) cm is cut from a cylindrical pine log. The log cross-section is a circle with diameter \(15\) cm, which is the diagonal of the rectangular beam. Beam strength is \(S=kd^2w\), where \(k\) is constant.

parts.stem: Show that S=k(225w−w³), given S=kd²w.
parts.hint: Use the rectangle diagonal relation w²+d²=15² to express d², then apply the given strength relationship. Then substitute this into the given strength formula.

steps.explain: The rectangle diagonal is the circle diameter 15 cm, so the Pythagorean theorem gives w²+d²=225.

steps.explain: Rearrange to express depth squared.
The strength is S=kd²w. Substitute d²=225−w².
Expand.

parts.stem: What numerical dimensions give a beam of maximum strength?
parts.hint: Maximize S=k(225w−w³) for 0<w<15, then find d from w²+d²=225.

steps.explain: Since k>0, maximize g(w)=225w−w³.

steps.explain: Differentiate and set equal to zero.
The positive width is w=5√3 cm.

questions.stem: Given \( f'(3) = 0 \), note that \( f(x) = x^3 - 27x \) has a stationary point at \( x = 3 \). Then evaluate \( f''(3) \) to determine whether this stationary point is a maximum, minimum, or a horizontal point of inflection.

questions.stem: Given \( f'(3) = 0 \), note that \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 \) has a stationary point at \( x = 3 \). Then evaluate \( f''(3) \) to determine whether this stationary point is a maximum, minimum, or a horizontal point of inflection.

steps.explain: Differentiate \( f(x) \) and set \( f'(x)=0 \) to find the stationary points.
Differentiate again to test the nature of each stationary point using the second derivative.
Test \( x=3 \): since \( f''(3)=12(3)(1)=36>0 \), the curve is concave up there, so this is a local minimum. Substitute \( x=3 \) into \( f(x) \) for the y-value.

Test \( x=0 \): since \( f''(0)=0 \), the second-derivative test is inconclusive, so check the sign of \( f'(x) \) either side of \( x=0 \). Since \( f'(x)=4x^2(x-3) \) is negative on both sides of \( x=0 \) (the \( x^2 \) factor never changes sign), \( f' \) does not change sign — so this is a stationary point of inflection, not a turning point.

Also check where \( f''(x)=0 \) for any additional (non-stationary) inflection points: \( f''(x)=12x(x-2)=0 \) gives \( x=0 \) (already found) and \( x=2 \). Since \( f'(2)=4(4)(-1)=-16\ne0 \), this is a non-stationary inflection point.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the graph of a function f(x). The graph has a horizontal point of inflexion at A, a point of inflexion at B and a maximum turning point at C. Sketch the graph of the derivative f′(x).
questions.answer: The derivative touches zero at A without changing sign, has a local maximum at B, crosses zero from positive to negative at C, then remains negative.
questions.hint: Translate the graph features: a horizontal stationary inflection makes f′=0 without a sign change; an inflection of f makes a turning point of f′; a maximum makes f′ cross from positive to negative.

steps.explain: At A, f has a horizontal tangent and continues increasing. Thus f′(A)=0, but f′ stays positive on both sides: its graph touches the x-axis there.

steps.explain: At C, f has a maximum and a horizontal tangent. The slope changes from positive to negative, so f′ crosses the x-axis at C.

questions.stem: Using the methods of analysis for polynomial curve sketching, find the key features of the quartic curve \( y = 3x^4 - 16x^3 + 24x^2 + 10 \) and sketch it.

parts.stem: a) Which of the following correctly summarizes the key features of \( y = 3x^4 - 16x^3 + 24x^2 + 10 \)?
options: Horizontal point of inflection at (0, 10), local minimum at (2, 26).
Local minimum at (0, 10), local maximum at (2, 26).
Local minimum at (0, 10), horizontal point of inflection at (2, 26).
Local maximum at (0, 10), horizontal point of inflection at (2, 26).

steps.explain: Find the first derivative.
Find stationary points.
Find the second derivative to determine nature.
Evaluate.
steps.work: \text{At } x = 0, y''(0) = 48 > 0 \implies (0,10) \text{ is a local minimum.} \\ \text{At } x = 2, y''(2) = 36(4) - 96(2) + 48 = 144 - 192 + 48 = 0. \\ \text{Check } y': 12x(x-2)^2 \text{ is positive for } x > 0. \text{ The gradient does not change sign across } x=2 \text{, so } (2,26) \text{ is a horizontal point of inflection.}

ext.ans: Local minimum at (0, 10), horizontal point of inflection at (2, 26).

parts.stem: b) Sketch the graph of the function.
parts.answer: Sketch the quartic curve.

steps.explain: Plot stationary points.

questions.stem: For the rational function \( f(x) = \frac{2}{x^2 - 9} \), complete the following systematic curve sketching analysis.

parts.stem: a) Which of the following correctly gives the derivative of \( f(x) = \frac{2}{x^2 - 9} \)?

steps.explain: Rewrite the function using negative exponents.
Differentiate using the chain rule.

parts.stem: b) Show that \( y = f(x) \) has a stationary point at \( x = 0 \). Determine its nature using a slope table. (Format: '(0,-2/9) is a maximum')

steps.explain: Find stationary points by setting \( f'(x) = 0 \).
Find the corresponding y-coordinate.
Use a slope table to determine its nature.
steps.work: \begin{aligned} \text{For } x < 0 \; (\text{e.g., } x = -1): f'(-1) &= -\frac{4(-1)}{(-1^2 - 9)^2} = \frac{4}{64} > 0 \; (\text{rising}) \\ \text{For } x > 0 \; (\text{e.g., } x = 1): f'(1) &= -\frac{4(1)}{(1^2 - 9)^2} = -\frac{4}{64} < 0 \; (\text{falling}) \end{aligned}

steps.explain: Conclude.
steps.work: \text{Since the gradient changes from positive to negative, the point is a local maximum.}

parts.stem: c) Show that the function is even. What sort of symmetry does its graph have?
options: The function is even because \( f(-x) = -f(x) \). It is symmetric about the x-axis.
The function is odd because \( f(-x) = -f(x) \). It has rotational point symmetry.
The function is even because \( f(-x) = f(x) \). It is symmetric about the y-axis.
The function is neither odd nor even.

steps.explain: Substitute \( -x \) into \( f(x) \).
State the symmetry.
steps.work: \text{Since } f(-x) = f(x) \text{, the function is even. Even functions are symmetric under reflection across the y-axis.}

parts.stem: d) State the domain of the function and the equations of any vertical asymptotes. (Format: 'domain: x not equal to -3 or 3; vertical asymptotes: x = -3, x = 3')
options: domain: \( x \neq -3, 3 \); vertical asymptotes: \( x = -3, x = 3 \)
domain: all real \( x \); no vertical asymptotes

steps.explain: Find where the denominator is zero.
State the domain and asymptotes.
steps.work: \text{The function is undefined at } x = 3, -3 \text{. Therefore, the domain is all real } x \neq -3, 3 \text{ and the vertical asymptotes are the lines } x = 3 \text{ and } x = -3.

parts.stem: e) What value does \( f(x) \) approach as \( x \to \infty \) and as \( x \to -\infty \)? Hence write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote.

steps.explain: Evaluate the limit as \( x \to \pm\infty \).
Identify the horizontal asymptote.
steps.work: \text{Since the function approaches 0 as } x \text{ gets very large in either direction, the horizontal asymptote is } y = 0.

parts.stem: f) Sketch the graph of \( y = f(x) \), showing all important features.
parts.answer: Three branches separated by vertical asymptotes x = -3 and x = 3, with a local maximum in the middle branch at (0, -2/9), and y = 0 as the horizontal asymptote.

steps.work: \text{Draw dashed vertical lines at } x = -3 \text{ and } x = 3 \text{, and a dashed horizontal line at } y = 0.

steps.explain: Observe the sketched graph.
steps.work: \text{The middle branch covers all values from } -\infty \text{ up to the maximum } y = -\frac{2}{9}. \text{ The outer branches cover all positive y-values above the horizontal asymptote } y = 0.

questions.stem: For the rational function \( f(x) = \frac{2x}{x^2 - 9} \), complete the following systematic curve sketching analysis.

parts.stem: a) Show that the derivative of \( f(x) = \frac{2x}{x^2 - 9} \) is \( f'(x) = -\frac{2(x^2 + 9)}{(x^2 - 9)^2} \).

steps.explain: Use the quotient rule.
steps.work: \begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \frac{v u' - u v'}{v^2} \\ u &= 2x \implies u' = 2 \\ v &= x^2 - 9 \implies v' = 2x \end{aligned}

steps.explain: Substitute into the formula.

parts.stem: b) Why does the curve \( y = f(x) \) have no stationary points, and why is it always decreasing?
options: Because \( f'(x) > 0 \) for all \( x \) in the domain.
Because the numerator of \( f'(x) \) is zero.
Because \( f'(x) < 0 \) for all \( x \) in the domain.
Because \( f'(x) = 0 \) has no real solutions, and \( f'(x) > 0 \).

steps.explain: Analyze the sign of \( f'(x) \).
Evaluate the numerator and denominator.
steps.work: \text{For all real } x, x^2 + 9 \ge 9 > 0. \text{ Also, } (x^2 - 9)^2 > 0 \text{ for all } x \text{ in the domain.} \\ \implies \frac{2(x^2 + 9)}{(x^2 - 9)^2} \text{ is always positive.}

steps.explain: Conclude.
steps.work: \text{Thus, } f'(x) \text{ is always strictly negative. The curve has no turning points and is always decreasing.}

questions.stem: Consider the curve \(y=\sin x+\cos x\) in the domain \(-\pi \le x \le \pi\).

parts.stem: (a) Find the \(x\)-intercepts, expressed in terms of \(\pi\).
parts.hint: Set \(y=0\), rearrange to \(\tan x = -1\), then find all solutions within the given domain.

steps.explain: Set \(y=0\) and rearrange.
Solve \(\tan x=-1\) within \(-\pi \le x \le \pi\): tangent is negative in quadrants 2 and 4, with reference angle \(\pi/4\).

parts.stem: (b) Find any stationary points, and determine their nature.
parts.hint: Set \(y'=\cos x-\sin x=0\), solve for \(x\), then use \(y''\) to test the nature of each.

steps.explain: Differentiate and set \(y'=0\).
Solve within the domain: tangent is positive in quadrants 1 and 3.
Find the \(y\)-value at each: \(y(\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/4)+\cos(\pi/4)=\sqrt2\); \(y(-3\pi/4)=-\sqrt2\).
Use \(y''=-\sin x-\cos x\) to test nature: at \(x=\pi/4\), \(y''=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}<0\) (max); at \(x=-3\pi/4\), \(y''=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}>0\) (min).
steps.work: \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\sqrt2\right)\) is a maximum; \(\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4},-\sqrt2\right)\) is a minimum

parts.stem: (c) Find any points of inflection.
parts.hint: Set \(y''=0\) and solve, then confirm concavity actually changes sign either side.

steps.explain: Set \(y''=-\sin x-\cos x=0\) and rearrange.
This gives the same solutions as part (a): \(x=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) or \(x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).

Testing concavity either side of each (using a sign table for \(y''\)) confirms concavity changes at both — genuine points of inflection. Both happen to also be the \(x\)-intercepts from part (a), so \(y=0\) there.
steps.work: Concavity changes at both points, confirming inflection; \(y=0\) at each (from part a)

steps.explain: State both points of inflection.

parts.stem: (d) Explain why the points found in (c) are not points of horizontal inflection.

steps.explain: A point of inflection is "horizontal" only when the tangent at that point is also horizontal, i.e. \(y'=0\) there as well as \(y''=0\).
steps.work: Horizontal inflection requires BOTH \(y'=0\) AND \(y''=0\) at the same point

steps.explain: At \(x=-\pi/4\): \(y' = \cos(-\pi/4)-\sin(-\pi/4) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \sqrt2 \ne 0\). The tangent has a non-zero gradient there.
Since the gradient is not zero at these inflection points, the tangent is sloped (not horizontal) — so these are ordinary points of inflection, not horizontal ones.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) not points of horizontal inflection, since \(y'\ne0\) there

questions.stem: The graph y = f(x) in the diagram has a stationary point when x = 1, a point of inflexion when x = 3, and a horizontal asymptote y = −2. Sketch the graph y = f′(x), clearly indicating its features at x = 1 and x = 3, and the shape of the graph as x → ∞.
questions.answer: f′ crosses zero at x=1 from positive to negative; it has a local minimum at x=3; and it approaches 0 from below as x→∞.
questions.hint: A stationary maximum of f makes f′ cross the axis. An inflection of f makes f′ turn. A horizontal asymptote means the gradient tends to zero.

steps.explain: The graph of f rises before its maximum at x=1 and falls after it. Therefore f′ is positive before 1, zero at 1, and negative after 1.

steps.work: \(f\prime\prime\text{ changes sign at }3\Rightarrow f\prime\text{ has a local minimum at }3\)

steps.explain: As f approaches the horizontal asymptote y=−2, its slope approaches zero. Since f is still decreasing, f′ approaches zero from below.

questions.answer: f has a local minimum at x=5 because f′ changes from negative to positive there.
questions.hint: A local minimum of f occurs where f′ changes sign from negative to positive. Read where the gradient graph crosses the x-axis in that direction.

steps.explain: The graph is f′(x). It crosses the horizontal axis at x=1 and x=5.

questions.stem: For all x in the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, a function g(x) satisfies g′(x) < 0 and g′′(x) < 0. Sketch a possible graph of y = g(x) in this domain.
questions.answer: A decreasing curve that is concave down throughout 0≤x≤4.
questions.hint: g′<0 means the curve slopes downward. g′′<0 means the slope becomes more negative as x increases, so the curve bends downward.

steps.explain: Because g′(x)<0 at every point, g must decrease from left to right.
Because g′′(x)<0, the gradient itself decreases as x increases. Make the downward slope steeper toward x=4.

questions.stem: The number of unemployed people u at time t was studied over a period of time. At the start of this period, the number of unemployed was 800000.

parts.stem: Throughout the period, du/dt < 0. What does this say about the number of people unemployed during the period?

options.text: It stayed constant throughout the period.
It decreased at an increasing rate throughout the period.

parts.hint: The sign of du/dt tells whether u rises or falls as time increases.

steps.explain: The derivative du/dt is the slope of the graph of u against t.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 280"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M50 230H405M82 250V24" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M83 55 C105 126 143 169 197 190 C261 214 324 220 398 222" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="73" y="24" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">u</text><text x="401" y="247" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">t</text><text x="50" y="48" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">800 000</text></svg>

steps.explain: A negative slope means u gets smaller as time passes.
So the number unemployed decreased during the period.

parts.stem: It is also observed that, throughout the period, d²u/dt² > 0. Sketch this graph of u against t.
parts.answer: A decreasing curve that is concave up, starting at (0, 800000) and flattening as t increases.
parts.hint: Use both derivative signs: the first derivative makes the curve decrease; the positive second derivative means its negative slope becomes less steep.

steps.explain: The starting value fixes the first point at (0,800000).

parts.hint: Set dy/dx=0. Use the second derivative to decide whether each stationary point is a maximum or minimum.

steps.explain: Differentiate the curve and factor.

parts.answer: The curve y=6x²−x³ passes through (0,0) and (6,0), has a minimum at (0,0), an inflection point at (2,16), and a maximum at (4,32).
parts.hint: Use the stationary points, inflection point, and intercepts to place and shape the curve. Factor y to find the other x-intercept.

steps.explain: The stationary points are (0,0), a local minimum, and (4,32), a local maximum.

questions.stem: For the curve shown in the graph, classify each labeled point \( A \) and \( B \) as one of the following: global maximum, global minimum, local maximum, local minimum, or horizontal point of inflection.
options: A: global maximum, B: local minimum
A: local minimum, B: local maximum
A: local maximum, B: global minimum
A: local maximum, B: local minimum
questions.solution: A: local maximum, B: local minimum

steps.explain: Examine point A.
steps.work: \text{Point } A \text{ is a 'peak' relative to its immediate neighbors, so it is a local maximum. It is not a global maximum because the curve rises higher elsewhere.}

steps.explain: Examine point B.
steps.work: \text{Point } B \text{ is a 'valley' relative to its neighbors, making it a local minimum. It is not a global minimum because the curve falls lower elsewhere.}

questions.stem: For the curve shown in the graph on the closed interval \( [0, 4] \), classify each labeled point \( C, D, E, \) and \( F \) as one of the following: global maximum, global minimum, local maximum, local minimum, or horizontal point of inflection.
options: C: local maximum, D: global minimum, E: global maximum, F: local minimum
C: local minimum, D: local maximum, E: global minimum, F: global maximum
C: global maximum, D: local minimum, E: local maximum, F: global minimum
C: local maximum, D: local minimum, E: global maximum, F: global minimum
questions.solution: C: local maximum, D: local minimum, E: global maximum, F: global minimum

steps.explain: Identify the global extrema on the closed interval.
steps.work: \text{The highest point on the entire interval } [0, 4] \text{ is } E \text{, making it the global maximum. The lowest point is } F \text{, making it the global minimum.}

steps.explain: Identify the local extrema.
steps.work: \text{Point } C \text{ is a peak relative to its surroundings but is lower than } E \text{, so it is a local maximum. Point } D \text{ is a valley but higher than } F \text{, so it is a local minimum.}

questions.stem: For the curve shown in the graph, classify each labeled point \( G \) and \( H \) as one of the following: global maximum, global minimum, local maximum, local minimum, or horizontal point of inflection.
options: G: horizontal point of inflection, H: global maximum
G: local maximum, H: local minimum
G: global maximum, H: horizontal point of inflection
G: global maximum, H: local minimum
questions.solution: G: global maximum, H: horizontal point of inflection

steps.explain: Examine point G.
steps.work: \text{Point } G \text{ is the highest point on the entire visible curve. Since the curve goes downwards on both sides, } G \text{ is a global maximum.}

steps.explain: Examine point H.
steps.work: \text{At point } H \text{, the curve flattens out (zero gradient) but continues to fall. This means concavity changes and the tangent is horizontal, so } H \text{ is a horizontal point of inflection.}

questions.stem: For the curve shown in the graph, classify each labeled point \( I \) and \( J \) as one of the following: global maximum, global minimum, local maximum, local minimum, or horizontal point of inflection.
options: I: horizontal point of inflection, J: global minimum
I: local maximum, J: global minimum
I: local minimum, J: global maximum
I: horizontal point of inflection, J: local minimum
questions.solution: I: horizontal point of inflection, J: global minimum

steps.explain: Examine point I.
steps.work: \text{At point } I \text{, the curve flattens momentarily (gradient is zero) and then continues to fall. Thus, it is a horizontal point of inflection.}

steps.explain: Examine point J.
steps.work: \text{Point } J \text{ is the absolute lowest point on the entire domain shown, making it the global minimum.}

questions.stem: Determine the global maximum and minimum values of \(y\) for the curve \(y = e^2 + e^x - xe^2\) in the domain \(0 \le x \le 5\). (Give your answers as exact values.)

steps.explain: The global max/min of a continuous curve on a closed domain occurs either at a stationary point or at an endpoint. First find the stationary point(s) by differentiating and setting \(y'=0\).
Solve \(y'=0\): since \(e^x\) is one-to-one, \(e^x=e^2 \implies x=2\), which lies inside the domain \([0,5]\).
Evaluate \(y\) at the stationary point and at both endpoints of the domain.
Compare all three values: \(y(2)=0\) is the smallest (global minimum), and since \(e^5-4e^2 \approx 118.85\) is far larger than \(e^2+1\approx 8.39\), \(y(5)\) is the largest (global maximum).

questions.stem: A small-sized home swimming pool contains 100 kL of water when full. A water pump cycles the water in and out of the pool through a filter for cleaning and treatment. The flow rate of the volume of water that the pump filters in and out of the swimming pool in kilolitres per minute (kL/min) is given by: \(\frac{dV}{dt}=-0.3\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\). Find the minimum volume of water in the pool during the pumping cycle. Leave your answer in terms of \(\pi\).
questions.hint: The volume reaches its minimum when the cosine term in the volume expression is −1.

keyPoints.text: minimum volume of water in the pool
keyPoints.note: Use dV/dt=0 to find candidate extrema during the cycle, then compare the volume values.

steps.explain: Use the volume function from the preceding part.
Since cosine is at least −1, the smallest possible bracket value occurs when cosine equals −1.
Substitute the minimum cosine value.
Leave the exact answer in terms of π and include units.

questions.stem: A particle P moves along a straight line for 8 seconds, starting at the fixed point S at time t = 0. At time t seconds, P is x(t) metres to the right of S. The graph of x(t) is shown in the diagram.

parts.stem: At approximately what times is the velocity of the particle equal to 0?
parts.hint: Velocity is the gradient of the displacement-time graph. It is zero where the graph has a horizontal tangent.

steps.explain: Look for horizontal tangents on x(t). They occur at the small local maximum and the broad local minimum.

parts.hint: Acceleration is the second derivative of displacement. It is zero at an inflection point where the curve changes concavity.

parts.stem: At approximately what time is the distance from S greatest?
parts.hint: Distance from S is |x(t)|. Compare the largest positive and negative displacement values.

steps.explain: The graph gives signed displacement from S. Distance is its absolute value, so compare the height above x=0 with the depth below x=0.

parts.hint: Velocity is the signed slope of x(t), not the height of the curve. Find where the tangent is steepest upward.

steps.explain: Compare tangent gradients on the graph. The particle has greatest velocity where the graph rises most steeply.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a sketch of the curve y = 6x² − x³. The curve cuts the x axis at L, and has a local maximum at M and a point of inflection at N.

parts.stem: Find the coordinates of L.
parts.hint: Set y=0 and factor the expression. The diagram identifies L as the non-origin x-intercept.

steps.explain: At an x-intercept, y=0. Factor the equation.

parts.stem: Find the coordinates of M.
parts.hint: At a local maximum the derivative is zero. Solve for the nonzero stationary x-value and substitute into y.

steps.explain: Differentiate the curve to obtain its gradient.

steps.explain: At a stationary point, set the derivative equal to zero. The non-origin solution is x=4.
Substitute x=4 into the original equation.
So the local maximum is at M=(4,32).

parts.hint: A point of inflection occurs where the second derivative is zero and changes sign.

steps.explain: Differentiate twice.

Substitute x=2 into y=6x²−x³.
Therefore N=(2,16).

questions.stem: Consider the curve given by y = x³ − 6x + 4.

parts.stem: Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.
parts.hint: Set y′=0 to find stationary x-values. Use y′′ to decide maximum or minimum, and substitute into y for coordinates.

steps.explain: Differentiate once.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 280"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M42 230H405M220 250V22" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M48 205 C87 182 117 112 155 82 C186 58 207 96 220 133 C237 183 262 209 291 184 C331 147 365 76 399 42" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="155" cy="82" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="291" cy="184" r="5" fill="#8b5cf6"/><circle cx="220" cy="133" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/><text x="155" y="70" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(−√2,4+4√2)</text><text x="295" y="203" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(√2,4−4√2)</text><text x="226" y="127" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(0,4)</text><text x="402" y="227" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x</text></svg>

steps.explain: Set the gradient to zero and solve.
The second derivative is 6x. At x=−√2 it is negative (maximum); at x=√2 it is positive (minimum).
Substitute each x-value into y=x³−6x+4. This gives the two coordinates shown.

parts.stem: Find the coordinates of any point of inflexion.
parts.hint: Set the second derivative equal to zero, then use the original curve to get y.

steps.explain: Differentiate twice to find where concavity may change.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 440 280"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M42 230H405M220 250V22" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M48 205 C87 182 117 112 155 82 C186 58 207 96 220 133 C237 183 262 209 291 184 C331 147 365 76 399 42" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="155" cy="82" r="5" fill="#ef4444"/><circle cx="291" cy="184" r="5" fill="#8b5cf6"/><circle cx="220" cy="133" r="5" fill="#f59e0b"/><text x="155" y="70" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(−√2,4+4√2)</text><text x="295" y="203" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(√2,4−4√2)</text><text x="226" y="127" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">(0,4)</text><text x="402" y="227" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">x</text></svg>

When x=0, y=0−0+4=4. The second derivative changes sign across zero, so this is an inflection point.

questions.stem: A function is given by f(x) = 3x⁴ + 4x³ − 12x².

parts.stem: A function is given by f(x) = 3x⁴ + 4x³ − 12x². Find the coordinates of the stationary points of f(x) and determine their nature.

steps.explain: Differentiate and factor.

parts.answer: A quartic opening upward at both ends, with stationary minimums at (−2,−32) and (1,−5), and stationary maximum at (0,0).
parts.hint: The leading coefficient is positive, so both ends rise. Plot the three stationary points and connect them smoothly in order.

steps.explain: Mark the stationary points from part (i).

Draw a smooth W-shaped curve through the minima and maximum.

parts.stem: For what values of x is the function increasing?
parts.hint: Use the factored derivative and make a sign chart around x=−2,0,1.

steps.explain: The derivative is 12x(x+2)(x−1). Its zeros divide the number line into four intervals.

steps.explain: Testing signs gives f′<0 for x<−2, f′>0 for −2<x<0, f′<0 for 0<x<1, and f′>0 for x>1.
The function increases where f′ is positive.

parts.stem: For what values of k will 3x⁴ + 4x³ − 12x² + k = 0 have no solution?
parts.hint: The equation is f(x)=−k. Use the global minimum value of f and decide when the horizontal line y=−k lies below the graph.

steps.explain: From part (i), the lowest stationary value is f(−2)=−32. Since both ends rise, this is the global minimum.

steps.explain: The equation f(x)+k=0 is equivalent to f(x)=−k, a horizontal line. There is no intersection only if −k lies below −32.
Reverse the inequality when multiplying by −1.
Thus the quartic equation has no real solution when k>32.

parts.stem: Show that f(x) is an even function.

Evaluate f: f(±2)=16−32=−16 and f(0)=0.
The second derivative is 12x²−16. It is positive at ±2 and negative at 0.
Thus the two outer points are minima and the origin is a maximum.

parts.answer: An even W-shaped quartic symmetric about the y-axis, crossing at x=±2√2 and touching the x-axis at its local maximum (0,0), with minima (±2,−16).
parts.hint: Use even symmetry, the intercepts and stationary points. Since the leading term is positive, both ends rise.

steps.explain: Because f is even, the left and right sides mirror across the y-axis.
