questions.stem: A farmer is fencing a paddock using P metres of fencing. The paddock is to be in the shape of a sector of a circle with radius r and sector angle θ in radians, as shown in the diagram.

parts.stem: Show that the length of fencing required to fence the perimeter of the paddock is P = r(θ + 2).
parts.hint: The perimeter has two straight radii and one arc. The arc length is rθ when θ is measured in radians.

steps.explain: The paddock perimeter includes the two straight sides, each of length r.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M90 210L110 92A120 120 0 0 1 285 210Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".42" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M90 210L110 92M90 210L285 210" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M117 199A28 28 0 0 1 113 182" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="90" cy="210" r="4" fill="#334155"/><text x="91" y="233" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">centre</text><text x="173" y="201" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="120" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text></svg>

steps.explain: For angle θ in radians, the curved arc length is rθ.
Add the straight sides and arc.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M90 210L110 92A120 120 0 0 1 285 210Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".42" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M90 210L110 92M90 210L285 210" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M117 199A28 28 0 0 1 113 182" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="90" cy="210" r="4" fill="#334155"/><text x="91" y="233" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">centre</text><text x="173" y="201" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="120" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text></svg>

parts.stem: Show that the area of the sector is A = (1/2)Pr − r².
parts.answer: A=Pr/2−r².
parts.hint: The sector area is (1/2)r²θ. Use θ=P/r−2 from the perimeter relation.

steps.explain: The sector area formula for radians is A=(1/2)r²θ.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M90 210L110 92A120 120 0 0 1 285 210Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".42" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M90 210L110 92M90 210L285 210" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M117 199A28 28 0 0 1 113 182" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="90" cy="210" r="4" fill="#334155"/><text x="91" y="233" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">centre</text><text x="173" y="201" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="120" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text></svg>

steps.explain: Rearrange P=r(θ+2) to find θ.
Substitute and simplify.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M90 210L110 92A120 120 0 0 1 285 210Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".42" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M90 210L110 92M90 210L285 210" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M117 199A28 28 0 0 1 113 182" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="90" cy="210" r="4" fill="#334155"/><text x="91" y="233" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">centre</text><text x="173" y="201" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="120" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text></svg>

parts.stem: Find the radius of the sector, in terms of P, that will maximise the area of the paddock.
parts.hint: Treat A=Pr/2−r² as a quadratic in r. Differentiate and set the derivative to zero.

steps.explain: Use the area expression from part (ii).

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M90 210L110 92A120 120 0 0 1 285 210Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".42" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M90 210L110 92M90 210L285 210" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M117 199A28 28 0 0 1 113 182" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="90" cy="210" r="4" fill="#334155"/><text x="91" y="233" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">centre</text><text x="173" y="201" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="120" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text></svg>

steps.explain: Differentiate with respect to r.
Set the derivative to zero and solve.
Since d²A/dr²=−2<0, the stationary value is a maximum.

parts.stem: Find the angle θ that gives the maximum area of the paddock.
parts.hint: Substitute the maximizing radius from part (iii) into θ=P/r−2.

steps.explain: Use θ=P/r−2 from the perimeter equation.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" viewBox="0 0 350 300"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="white"/><path d="M90 210L110 92A120 120 0 0 1 285 210Z" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity=".42" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M90 210L110 92M90 210L285 210" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="2.2"/><path d="M117 199A28 28 0 0 1 113 182" fill="none" stroke="#f59e0b" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="90" cy="210" r="4" fill="#334155"/><text x="91" y="233" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">centre</text><text x="173" y="201" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">r</text><text x="120" y="185" font-family="Arial" font-size="13">θ</text></svg>

steps.explain: Substitute r=P/4.
Thus the angle is 2 radians.

parts.stem: Explain why it is only possible to construct a paddock in the shape of a sector if P/[2(π+1)] < r < P/2.
parts.answer: A sector angle must satisfy 0<θ<2π. Substituting θ=P/r−2 gives P/[2(π+1)]<r<P/2.
parts.hint: A valid sector has positive angle less than a full turn. Apply 0<P/r−2<2π and solve carefully for positive r.

steps.explain: The central angle must be positive and less than a complete circle.

From the left inequality, P/r>2, so r<P/2.
From the right inequality, P/r<2π+2=2(π+1), so r>P/[2(π+1)].
Combine the strict bounds.

questions.stem: A rainwater tank is to be designed in the shape of a cylinder with radius r metres and height h metres. The volume of the tank is to be 10 cubic metres. Let A be the surface area of the tank, including its top and base, in square metres.

parts.stem: Given that A = 2πr² + 2πrh, show that A = 2πr² + 20/r.
parts.answer: A=2πr²+20/r.
parts.hint: Use the volume constraint πr²h=10 to express h in terms of r, then substitute into the surface-area formula.

steps.explain: The tank volume is 10 m³ and cylinder volume is πr²h.

parts.stem: New technology means that the cost of laying the cable underwater can be reduced to $1100 per kilometre. Determine the path for laying the cable in this case.

options.text: Lay along shore from P to R, then underwater from R to S.
Lay directly from P to S underwater.
Lay along shore from P to Q with x=5/4 km, then underwater to S.
Lay along shore from P to Q with x=30/√21 km, then underwater to S.

parts.hint: Use the new underwater rate in the cost function. Check the derivative over the allowed interval 0≤x≤5.

steps.explain: With the new rate, the total cost is 1000(5−x)+1100√(x²+9).

steps.explain: Differentiate.
For 0≤x≤5, the ratio x/√(x²+9) is at most 5/√34. Thus C′≤−1000+5500/√34<0 throughout.
The cost decreases as x increases across the whole shore interval, so choose x=5, meaning Q=R.
Therefore lay the cable along the shore from P to R, then underwater from R to S.

questions.stem: The diagram shows two parallel brick walls KJ and MN joined by a fence from J to M. The wall KJ is s metres long and ∠KJM=α. The fence JM is ℓ metres long. A new fence is to be built from K to a point P somewhere on MN. The new fence KP will cross the original fence JM at O. Let OJ=x metres, where 0<x<ℓ.

parts.stem: Show that the total area, A, enclosed by triangles ΔOKJ and ΔOMP is A = s(x − ℓ + ℓ²/(2x)) sin α.

parts.hint: Find the areas of the two triangles using 1/2 ab sin included angle. Use the similar triangles to express MP in terms of x and ℓ.

questions.stem:
Find the primitive of the function:
\( f(x) = x^5 \)
questions.hint: Use the power rule for integration: add 1 to the power and divide by the new power.

steps.explain: State the power rule for integration.
steps.work:
To find the primitive (integral), we use the power rule: add 1 to the exponent, then divide by the new exponent.
\[ \int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \]

steps.explain: Apply the rule to the given function.
steps.work:
For \( f(x) = x^5 \), the exponent is 5. We add 1 to get 6, and divide by 6:
\[ \int x^5 \, dx = \frac{x^{5+1}}{5+1} + C \]
\[ = \frac{x^6}{6} + C \]

questions.stem:
Find the primitive of the function:
\( f(x) = 4x \)
questions.hint: Integrate term-by-term. The primitive of x is x^2 / 2.

steps.explain: State the power rule for integration.
steps.work:
To find the primitive, we use the power rule. The coefficient 4 stays in front, and we integrate \( x^1 \).
\[ \int ax^n \, dx = a \left( \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \right) + C \]

steps.explain: Apply the rule to the given function.
steps.work:
For \( f(x) = 4x \), the exponent is 1. We add 1 to get 2, and divide by 2:
\[ \int 4x^1 \, dx = 4 \left( \frac{x^{1+1}}{1+1} \right) + C \]
\[ = \frac{4x^2}{2} + C \]
\[ = 2x^2 + C \]

questions.stem:
Find the primitive of the function:
\( f(x) = x^3 + x^5 \)
questions.hint: Integrate each term individually using the power rule.

steps.explain: Integrate the polynomial term by term.
steps.work:
We apply the power rule to each term individually.
\[ \int (x^3 + x^5) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:
Add 1 to the exponent of each term and divide by the new exponent:
\[ = \frac{x^{3+1}}{3+1} + \frac{x^{5+1}}{5+1} + C \]
\[ = \frac{x^4}{4} + \frac{x^6}{6} + C \]

questions.stem:
Find the primitive of the function:
\( f(x) = 3x^2 - 4x^3 \)
questions.hint: Integrate 3x^2 to x^3 and 4x^3 to x^4.

steps.explain: Integrate the polynomial term by term.
steps.work:
We apply the power rule to each term individually.
\[ \int (3x^2 - 4x^3) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:
Add 1 to the exponent of each term and divide by the new exponent:
\[ = \frac{3x^{2+1}}{2+1} - \frac{4x^{3+1}}{3+1} + C \]
\[ = \frac{3x^3}{3} - \frac{4x^4}{4} + C \]

steps.explain: Simplify the expression.
steps.work:
Simplify the fractions:
\[ = x^3 - x^4 + C \]

questions.stem:

steps.explain: Integrate the polynomial term by term.

We apply the power rule to each term individually. Remember that a constant \( k \) becomes \( kx \).
\[ \int (x^2 - 2x + 3) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:
Add 1 to the exponent of each term and divide by the new exponent:
\[ = \frac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} - \frac{2x^{1+1}}{1+1} + 3x + C \]
\[ = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{2x^2}{2} + 3x + C \]

questions.stem:

\( f(x) = 4 - 6x + 24x^7 \)

steps.explain: Integrate the polynomial term by term.
steps.work:
We apply the power rule to each term individually.
\[ \int (4 - 6x + 24x^7) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:
Add 1 to the exponent of each term and divide by the new exponent:
\[ = 4x - \frac{6x^{1+1}}{1+1} + \frac{24x^{7+1}}{7+1} + C \]
\[ = 4x - \frac{6x^2}{2} + \frac{24x^8}{8} + C \]

questions.stem:
Find \( y \) as a function of \( x \) if:
\( y' = 2x + 5 \) and \( y = 4 \) when \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Integrate y' to find the general form y = f(x) + C, then solve for C using the given point.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find \( y \), we must integrate the derivative function:
\[ y = \int (2x + 5) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate term by term.
steps.work:
Apply the power rule to each term and add the constant of integration \( C \):
\[ y = \frac{2x^2}{2} + 5x + C \]
\[ y = x^2 + 5x + C \]

steps.explain: Use the initial condition to find \( C \).
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 4 \) when \( x = 0 \). Substitute these values into the general equation:
\[ 4 = (0)^2 + 5(0) + C \]
\[ 4 = 0 + C \]
\[ C = 4 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 4 \) back into the equation:
\[ y = x^2 + 5x + 4 \]

questions.stem:
Find \( y \) as a function of \( x \) if:
\( y' = 2x + 5 \) and \( y = 10 \) when \( x = 1 \).
questions.hint: Integrate y' and then use the condition y(1) = 10 to find C.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find \( y \), we must integrate the derivative function:
\[ y = \int (2x + 5) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate term by term.
steps.work:
Apply the power rule to each term and add the constant of integration \( C \):
\[ y = \frac{2x^2}{2} + 5x + C \]
\[ y = x^2 + 5x + C \]

steps.explain: Use the initial condition to find \( C \).
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 10 \) when \( x = 1 \). Substitute these values into the general equation:
\[ 10 = (1)^2 + 5(1) + C \]
\[ 10 = 1 + 5 + C \]
\[ 10 = 6 + C \]
\[ C = 4 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 4 \) back into the equation:
\[ y = x^2 + 5x + 4 \]

questions.stem:
Find \( y \) as a function of \( x \) if:
\( y' = 6x^2 + 3 \) and \( y = 2 \) when \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Find the general antiderivative, then use the initial value at x = 0.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find \( y \), we must integrate the derivative function:
\[ y = \int (6x^2 + 3) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate term by term.
steps.work:
Apply the power rule to each term and add the constant of integration \( C \):
\[ y = \frac{6x^3}{3} + 3x + C \]
\[ y = 2x^3 + 3x + C \]

steps.explain: Use the initial condition to find \( C \).
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 2 \) when \( x = 0 \). Substitute these values:
\[ 2 = 2(0)^3 + 3(0) + C \]
\[ 2 = 0 + C \]
\[ C = 2 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 2 \) back into the equation:
\[ y = 2x^3 + 3x + 2 \]

questions.stem:
Find \( y \) as a function of \( x \) if:
\( y' = 6x^2 + 3 \) and \( y = 7 \) when \( x = 1 \).
questions.hint: Integrate the derivative first, then use y(1) = 7 to find C.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find \( y \), we must integrate the derivative function:
\[ y = \int (6x^2 + 3) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate term by term.
steps.work:
Apply the power rule to each term and add the constant of integration \( C \):
\[ y = \frac{6x^3}{3} + 3x + C \]
\[ y = 2x^3 + 3x + C \]

steps.explain: Use the initial condition to find \( C \).
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 7 \) when \( x = 1 \). Substitute these values:
\[ 7 = 2(1)^3 + 3(1) + C \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.

steps.explain: Use the initial condition to find \( C \).

\[ 1 = (0)^3 - 3(0)^2 + 4(0) + C \]

questions.stem:
Write the function using a fractional index, and hence find its primitive:
\( f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x} \)
questions.hint: Write root(3, x) as x^(1/3) and integrate.

steps.explain: Convert the root to a fractional index.
steps.work:
Rewrite the cube root as a fractional power:
\[ f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x} = x^{\frac{1}{3}} \]

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:
To integrate, we add 1 to the power and divide by the new power:
\[ \int x^{\frac{1}{3}} \, dx = \frac{x^{\frac{1}{3} + 1}}{\frac{1}{3} + 1} + C \]

steps.explain: Simplify the fraction addition.
steps.work:
To add 1 to the fraction, write it with a common denominator (\(1 = \frac{3}{3}\)):
\[ \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \]
So the expression becomes:
\[ = \frac{x^{\frac{4}{3}}}{\frac{4}{3}} + C \]

steps.explain: State the final expression.
steps.work:
Dividing by a fraction is mathematically identical to multiplying by its reciprocal (flip the fraction):
\[ = \frac{3}{4}x^{\frac{4}{3}} + C \]

questions.stem:

steps.explain: Convert the root to a fractional index.

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:

steps.explain: Simplify the fraction addition.

\[ -\frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{3} = \frac{2}{3} \]
So the expression becomes:
\[ = \frac{x^{\frac{2}{3}}}{\frac{2}{3}} + C \]

steps.explain: State the final expression.
steps.work:
Dividing by a fraction is mathematically identical to multiplying by its reciprocal (flip the fraction):
\[ = \frac{3}{2}x^{\frac{2}{3}} + C \]

questions.stem:
Write the function using a fractional index, and hence find its primitive:
\( f(x) = \frac{3}{\sqrt{x}} \)
questions.hint: Rewrite as 3x^(-1/2) and integrate.

steps.explain: Convert the root to a fractional index.
steps.work:
Rewrite the root in the denominator as a negative fractional power. The constant 3 stays in front:
\[ f(x) = \frac{3}{\sqrt{x}} = \frac{3}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}} = 3x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \]

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:
To integrate, we add 1 to the power and divide by the new power:
\[ \int 3x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \, dx = 3 \left( \frac{x^{-\frac{1}{2} + 1}}{-\frac{1}{2} + 1} \right) + C \]

steps.explain: Simplify the fraction addition.
steps.work:
Write 1 with a common denominator (\(1 = \frac{2}{2}\)):
\[ -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{2}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \]
So the expression becomes:
\[ = 3 \left( \frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} \right) + C \]

steps.explain: State the final expression.
steps.work:
Dividing by \( \frac{1}{2} \) is mathematically identical to multiplying by 2:
\[ = 3 \left( 2x^{\frac{1}{2}} \right) + C \]
\[ = 6x^{\frac{1}{2}} + C = 6\sqrt{x} + C \]

questions.stem:

steps.explain: Convert the root to a fractional index.

steps.explain: Apply the power rule.
steps.work:

Write 1 with a common denominator (\(1 = \frac{4}{4}\)):
\[ \frac{3}{4} + \frac{4}{4} = \frac{7}{4} \]
So the expression becomes:
\[ = \frac{x^{\frac{7}{4}}}{\frac{7}{4}} + C \]

steps.explain: State the final expression.
steps.work:
Dividing by a fraction is mathematically identical to multiplying by its reciprocal (flip the fraction):
\[ = \frac{4}{7}x^{\frac{7}{4}} + C \]

questions.stem:
Find \( y \) as a function of \( x \) if:
\( \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \) and \( y = 3 \) when \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Rewrite the derivative as x^(-1/2) and integrate. Then solve for C.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( \frac{dy}{dx} \):
\[ y = \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
First, rewrite the root as a fractional index: \( x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \).
Now integrate using the power rule:
\[ y = \frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} + C \]
\[ y = 2\sqrt{x} + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 3 \) when \( x = 0 \). Substitute these values into our general equation:
\[ 3 = 2\sqrt{0} + C \]
\[ 3 = 0 + C \]
\[ C = 3 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 3 \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = 2\sqrt{x} + 3 \]

questions.stem: Find the member of the family of curves with gradient function \( \frac{dy}{dx} = -2x \) that passes through the point \( A(1, 3) \).

steps.explain: Set up the integral.

\[ 3 = -(1)^2 + C \]
\[ 3 = -1 + C \]
\[ C = 4 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 4 \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = -x^2 + 4 \]

questions.stem:
Use the linear composite integration rule to find the primitive:
\( f(x) = (x+2)^3 \)
questions.hint: The primitive of (ax+b)^n is (ax+b)^(n+1) / a(n+1). Here, a = 1.

steps.explain: Identify the parameters for the composite rule.
steps.work:
For the function \((x-2)^4\), it is in the form \((ax+b)^n\).
Here, \(a = 1\) (the coefficient of \(x\)) and \(n = 4\) (the exponent).

steps.explain: Apply the composite integration rule.
steps.work:
The rule is:
\[ \int (ax+b)^n \, dx = \frac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)} + C \]
Substitute our values into the formula:
\[ = \frac{(x-2)^{4+1}}{1(4+1)} + C \]

steps.explain: Simplify the arithmetic.
steps.work:
Calculate the numbers in the exponent and the denominator:
\[ = \frac{(x-2)^5}{1(5)} + C \]
\[ = \frac{(x-2)^5}{5} + C \]

steps.explain: Simplify the arithmetic.

questions.stem: Find \( y \) if \( y' = (x-2)^4 \), given that \( y = 3 \) when \( x = 2 \).
questions.hint: Integrate composite linear function and solve for C with initial coordinates.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( y' \):
\[ y = \int (x-2)^4 \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Use the composite integration rule \( \int (ax+b)^n \, dx = \frac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)} \):
\[ y = \frac{(x-2)^5}{(1)(5)} + C \]
\[ y = \frac{(x-2)^5}{5} + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 3 \) when \( x = 2 \). Substitute these values into our general equation:
\[ 3 = \frac{(2-2)^5}{5} + C \]
\[ 3 = \frac{0^5}{5} + C \]
\[ 3 = 0 + C \]
\[ C = 3 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 3 \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = \frac{(x-2)^5}{5} + 3 \]

questions.stem: Find \( y \) if \( y' = (3x+1)^3 \), given that \( y = -2 \) when \( x = 0 \).

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( y' \):
\[ y = \int (3x+1)^3 \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Use the composite integration rule. Remember to multiply the denominator by the inner derivative (3):
\[ y = \frac{(3x+1)^4}{(3)(4)} + C \]
\[ y = \frac{(3x+1)^4}{12} + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = -\frac{25}{12} \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = \frac{(3x+1)^4}{12} - \frac{25}{12} \]

questions.stem: Find \( y \) if \( y' = \sqrt{3x+1} \), given that \( y = 1 \) when \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Integrate composite root to power 3/2, dividing by 3 * (3/2) = 9/2.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( y' \):
\[ y = \int \sqrt{3x+1} \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Rewrite as a fractional index \( (3x+1)^{\frac{1}{2}} \) and use the composite rule:
\[ y = \frac{(3x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(3)(\frac{3}{2})} + C \]
\[ y = \frac{(3x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{9}{2}} + C \]
\[ y = \frac{2}{9}(3x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 1 \) when \( x = 0 \). Substitute these values:
\[ 1 = \frac{2}{9}(3(0)+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \]
\[ 1 = \frac{2}{9}(1)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \]
\[ 1 = \frac{2}{9} + C \]
\[ C = 1 - \frac{2}{9} = \frac{7}{9} \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = \frac{7}{9} \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = \frac{2}{9}(3x+1)^{\frac{3}{2}} + \frac{7}{9} \]

questions.stem:
Find the equation of the curve through the origin whose gradient is:
\( \frac{dy}{dx} = 5x^4 - 3x^2 + 2 \)
questions.hint: Origin coordinates are (0, 0). Integrate and solve for C.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( \frac{dy}{dx} \):
\[ y = \int (5x^4 - 3x^2 + 2) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Integrate term by term using the power rule:
\[ y = \frac{5x^5}{5} - \frac{3x^3}{3} + 2x + C \]
\[ y = x^5 - x^3 + 2x + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
The curve passes through the origin \( (0,0) \), meaning \( y = 0 \) when \( x = 0 \). Substitute these values:
\[ 0 = (0)^5 - (0)^3 + 2(0) + C \]
\[ 0 = 0 + C \]
\[ C = 0 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Since \( C = 0 \), the final equation is:
\[ y = x^5 - x^3 + 2x \]

questions.stem:
Find the curve passing through \( (2, 5) \) with gradient function:
\( \frac{dy}{dx} = 3 + 4x - 3x^2 \)
questions.hint: Integrate and use condition y(2) = 5 to find C.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( \frac{dy}{dx} \):
\[ y = \int (3 + 4x - 3x^2) \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Integrate term by term using the power rule:
\[ y = 3x + \frac{4x^2}{2} - \frac{3x^3}{3} + C \]
\[ y = 3x + 2x^2 - x^3 + C \]
\[ y = -x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
The curve passes through \( (2,5) \), meaning \( y = 5 \) when \( x = 2 \). Substitute these values:
\[ 5 = -(2)^3 + 2(2)^2 + 3(2) + C \]
\[ 5 = -8 + 8 + 6 + C \]
\[ 5 = 6 + C \]
\[ C = -1 \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = -1 \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = -x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x - 1 \]

questions.stem:
Find the curve through the point \( (\frac{1}{3}, 2) \) with gradient function:
\( y' = (2-3x)^3 \)
questions.hint: Use linear composite integration and substitute coordinates to solve for C.

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the curve \( y \), we integrate the gradient function \( y' \):
\[ y = \int (2-3x)^3 \, dx \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Use the composite integration rule. Remember to divide by the inner derivative (-3):
\[ y = \frac{(2-3x)^4}{(-3)(4)} + C \]
\[ y = -\frac{(2-3x)^4}{12} + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
The curve passes through \( (\frac{1}{3}, 2) \), meaning \( y = 2 \) when \( x = \frac{1}{3} \). Substitute these values:
\[ 2 = -\frac{(2 - 3(\frac{1}{3}))^4}{12} + C \]
\[ 2 = -\frac{(2 - 1)^4}{12} + C \]
\[ 2 = -\frac{1}{12} + C \]
\[ C = 2 + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{25}{12} \]

steps.explain: State the final equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = \frac{25}{12} \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = -\frac{(2-3x)^4}{12} + \frac{25}{12} \]

questions.stem: Find \( y \) if \( \frac{dy}{dt} = 4t^3 - 6t^2 + 3 \), and \( y = 5 \) when \( t = 0 \). Hence, find the value of \( y \) when \( t = 2 \).
questions.hint: Integrate to get y(t), solve for C, then evaluate y(2).

steps.explain: Set up the integral.
steps.work:
To find the equation for \( y \), we integrate the derivative \( \frac{dy}{dt} \):
\[ y = \int (4t^3 - 6t^2 + 3) \, dt \]

steps.explain: Integrate to find the general equation.
steps.work:
Integrate term by term:
\[ y = \frac{4t^4}{4} - \frac{6t^3}{3} + 3t + C \]
\[ y = t^4 - 2t^3 + 3t + C \]

steps.explain: Solve for the constant C.
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 5 \) when \( t = 0 \). Substitute these values:
\[ 5 = (0)^4 - 2(0)^3 + 3(0) + C \]
\[ 5 = 0 + C \]
\[ C = 5 \]

The specific equation is \( y = t^4 - 2t^3 + 3t + 5 \).

steps.explain: Find the value of y when t = 2.

questions.stem: Explain why the rule for finding the primitive of \( x^n \), which is \( \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \) (for \( n \ne -1 \)), cannot be applied when \( n = -1 \).
options: Because substituting \( n = -1 \) yields a division by zero in the denominator, which is mathematically undefined.
Because substituting \( n = -1 \) results in a negative area under the curve.
Because substituting \( n = -1 \) makes the numerator zero, which violates the power rule.
Because the power rule only works for positive integers.
questions.hint: Look at what happens to the denominator when you plug in n = -1.
questions.solution: Substituting n = -1 yields division by zero in the fraction, which is mathematically undefined.

steps.explain: Write down the power rule formula.
steps.work:
The power rule for integration states that to find the primitive of \( x^n \), we add 1 to the power and divide by the new power:
\[ \int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \]

steps.explain: Substitute n = -1 into the formula.
steps.work:
Let's try to apply this rule blindly when \( n = -1 \) (which represents \( \frac{1}{x} \)):
\[ \int x^{-1} \, dx = \frac{x^{-1+1}}{-1+1} + C \]

steps.explain: Simplify the mathematical expression.
steps.work:
Simplify the mathematical operations in the exponent and the denominator:
\[ \int x^{-1} \, dx = \frac{x^0}{0} + C \]
\[ \int x^{-1} \, dx = \frac{1}{0} + C \]

steps.explain: Conclude using the rules of mathematics.
steps.work:
In mathematics, division by zero is strictly undefined. Because applying the formula results in a zero in the denominator (\( \frac{1}{0} \)), the power rule completely breaks down and cannot be used here.

*(Note: This is why the primitive of \( x^{-1} \) is defined separately using the natural logarithm: \( \ln|x| + C \)).*

questions.stem: Find \( y \) as a function of \( x \) if \( y'' = 12x + 2 \), given that when \( x = 1 \), \( y' = 5 \) and \( y = 3 \).
questions.hint: Integrate twice. Find the constant of integration for y' first, then integrate again to find the constant for y.

steps.explain: Integrate y'' to find y'.
steps.work:
The second derivative is \( y'' = 12x + 2 \). To find the first derivative \( y' \), we integrate:
\[ y' = \int (12x + 2) \, dx \]
\[ y' = \frac{12x^2}{2} + 2x + C_1 \]
\[ y' = 6x^2 + 2x + C_1 \]

steps.explain: Solve for C1 using the first initial condition.
steps.work:
We are given that \( y' = 5 \) when \( x = 1 \). Substitute these values to find \( C_1 \):
\[ 5 = 6(1)^2 + 2(1) + C_1 \]
\[ 5 = 6 + 2 + C_1 \]
\[ 5 = 8 + C_1 \]
\[ C_1 = -3 \]
So, the equation for the first derivative is:
\[ y' = 6x^2 + 2x - 3 \]

steps.explain: Integrate y' to find y.
steps.work:
Now, integrate the first derivative to find the original function \( y \):
\[ y = \int (6x^2 + 2x - 3) \, dx \]
\[ y = \frac{6x^3}{3} + \frac{2x^2}{2} - 3x + C_2 \]
\[ y = 2x^3 + x^2 - 3x + C_2 \]

steps.explain: Solve for C2 using the second initial condition.
steps.work:
We are given that \( y = 3 \) when \( x = 1 \). Substitute these values to find \( C_2 \):
\[ 3 = 2(1)^3 + (1)^2 - 3(1) + C_2 \]
\[ 3 = 2 + 1 - 3 + C_2 \]
\[ 3 = 0 + C_2 \]
\[ C_2 = 3 \]

Substitute \( C_2 = 3 \) back into the equation for our final answer:
\[ y = 2x^3 + x^2 - 3x + 3 \]

questions.stem: A function \( f(x) \) has second derivative \( f''(x) = 2x - 6 \). Its graph passes through the point \( (3, 20) \), and at this point the tangent has a gradient of \( 11 \). Complete parts a), b), and c).

parts.stem: a) Find \( f'(x) \).

Substitute coordinates x = 3 and tangent gradient = 11
Solve for the constant C1

parts.stem: b) Find \( f(x) \).

Substitute the point (3, 20) to find C2
Solve for the constant C2

parts.stem: c) Find the y-intercept of the curve.

steps.explain: Find the y-intercept
steps.work:
The y-intercept occurs when \( x = 0 \). Substitute \( x = 0 \) into the equation for \( f(x) \):
\[ f(0) = \frac{0^3}{3} - 3(0)^2 + 20(0) - 22 \]
\[ f(0) = -22 \]
Thus, the y-intercept is \( (0, -22) \).

questions.stem: If \( y'' = 12 - 6x \), complete parts a) and b).

parts.stem: a) Find the general equation for \( y \), using integration constants \( C \) and \( D \).

steps.explain: Integrate y'' to find the first derivative y'.
steps.work:
The second derivative is \( y'' = 12 - 6x \). Integrate it to find \( y' \):
\[ y' = \int (12 - 6x) \, dx \]
\[ y' = 12x - \frac{6x^2}{2} + C \]
\[ y' = 12x - 3x^2 + C \]

steps.explain: Integrate y' to find the general equation for y.
steps.work:
Now integrate \( y' \) to find \( y \). Remember to add a second constant \( D \):
\[ y = \int (12x - 3x^2 + C) \, dx \]
\[ y = \frac{12x^2}{2} - \frac{3x^3}{3} + Cx + D \]
\[ y = 6x^2 - x^3 + Cx + D \]
\[ y = -x^3 + 6x^2 + Cx + D \]

parts.stem: b) Hence find the exact equation of the curve given that it passes through the points \( (1, 10) \) and \( (-1, 2) \).

steps.explain: Substitute the first point (1, 10) to create Equation 1.
steps.work:
We know the curve passes through \( (1, 10) \). Substitute \( x = 1, y = 10 \) into our general equation:
\[ 10 = -(1)^3 + 6(1)^2 + C(1) + D \]
\[ 10 = -1 + 6 + C + D \]
\[ 10 = 5 + C + D \]
\[ C + D = 5 \quad \text{--- (Equation 1)} \]

steps.explain: Substitute the second point (-1, 2) to create Equation 2.
Solve the simultaneous equations for C and D.
steps.work:
We have a system of linear equations:
1) \( C + D = 5 \)
2) \( -C + D = -5 \)

Add Equation 1 and Equation 2 together:
\[ (C + D) + (-C + D) = 5 + (-5) \]
\[ 2D = 0 \implies D = 0 \]

Substitute \( D = 0 \) back into Equation 1:
\[ C + 0 = 5 \implies C = 5 \]

steps.explain: State the final curve equation.
steps.work:
Substitute \( C = 5 \) and \( D = 0 \) back into the general equation:
\[ y = -x^3 + 6x^2 + 5x + 0 \]
\[ y = -x^3 + 6x^2 + 5x \]

questions.stem: Consider the derivative \( f'(x) = -\frac{4}{x^2} \). We know that a continuous curve passing through \( A(2, 3) \) has equation \( y = \frac{4}{x} + 1 \). This is not strictly true, because the asymptote at \( x = 0 \) allows the two branches of the curve to move independently so that each branch has its own arbitrary constant. Complete parts a), b), and c).

parts.stem: a) Find \( g'(x) \) for the piecewise-defined function \( g(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{4}{x} + 1, & \text{for } x > 0 \\ \frac{4}{x} + 5, & \text{for } x < 0 \end{cases} \).
options: \( g'(x) = -\frac{4}{x^2} \text{ for } x > 0, \text{ and } g'(x) = -\frac{4}{x^2} + 4 \text{ for } x < 0 \)

steps.explain: Differentiate the first branch (x > 0).
steps.work:
For \( x > 0 \), the function is \( g(x) = 4x^{-1} + 1 \). Using the power rule:
\[ g'(x) = -4x^{-2} + 0 = -\frac{4}{x^2} \]

steps.explain: Differentiate the second branch (x < 0).
steps.work:
For \( x < 0 \), the function is \( g(x) = 4x^{-1} + 5 \). Using the power rule:
\[ g'(x) = -4x^{-2} + 0 = -\frac{4}{x^2} \]

steps.explain: Combine the results.
steps.work:
Since both branches have the exact same derivative, we can combine them and write:
\[ g'(x) = -\frac{4}{x^2} \quad \text{for all } x \neq 0 \]

parts.stem: b) Which of the following points does the graph of \( g(x) \) pass through?

steps.explain: Check the given points against the piecewise function conditions.
steps.work: The function \( g(x) \) uses different formulas depending on whether the x-coordinate is positive or negative.

steps.explain: Evaluate point A(2, 3).
steps.work:
For \( x = 2 \), since \( 2 > 0 \), we must use the top branch \( g(x) = \frac{4}{x} + 1 \).
\[ g(2) = \frac{4}{2} + 1 \]
\[ g(2) = 2 + 1 = 3 \]
This matches the y-coordinate of \( A(2, 3) \), so the graph correctly passes through this point.

parts.stem: c) Find the piecewise-defined equation of the function \( h(x) \) with the same derivative \( h'(x) = -\frac{4}{x^2} \) passing through the points \( A(1, 6) \) and \( B(-2, 1) \).

steps.explain: Set up the general piecewise function for h(x).
steps.work:
Since the derivative is \( h'(x) = -\frac{4}{x^2} \) for all \( x \neq 0 \), we integrate it to find the general branches. Because of the asymptote at \( x=0 \), each branch gets its own independent constant:
\[ h(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{4}{x} + C_1, & \text{for } x > 0 \\ \frac{4}{x} + C_2, & \text{for } x < 0 \end{cases} \]

steps.explain: Solve for C1 using point A(1, 6).
steps.work:
Point A has \( x = 1 \). Since \( 1 > 0 \), we must use the top branch and substitute \( (1, 6) \):
\[ 6 = \frac{4}{1} + C_1 \]
\[ 6 = 4 + C_1 \]
\[ C_1 = 2 \]

steps.explain: Solve for C2 using point B(-2, 1).
steps.work:
Point B has \( x = -2 \). Since \( -2 < 0 \), we must use the bottom branch and substitute \( (-2, 1) \):
\[ 1 = \frac{4}{-2} + C_2 \]
\[ 1 = -2 + C_2 \]
\[ C_2 = 3 \]

steps.explain: State the final piecewise function.
steps.work:
Substitute the constants back into the original branches to get the final answer:
\[ h(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{4}{x} + 2, & \text{for } x > 0 \\ \frac{4}{x} + 3, & \text{for } x < 0 \end{cases} \]

questions.stem: The graph of the gradient function \( y=f'(x) \) is a step function: \( f'(x)=-2 \) for \( x\lt 2 \) and \( f'(x)=2 \) for \( x\gt 2 \) (open circles at \( x=2 \)). Sketch a possible function \( y=f(x) \) that could have this gradient function.
questions.answer: f(x)=2|x-2|, a V-shaped graph with a corner (cusp) at (2,0), sloping down at gradient -2 for x<2 and up at gradient +2 for x>2, e.g. through (0,4) and (4,4).

steps.explain: Since \( f'(x)=-2 \) (constant negative gradient) for \( x\lt 2 \), \( f \) must be a straight line of slope \( -2 \) on that interval.

steps.explain: Since \( f'(x)=2 \) (constant positive gradient) for \( x\gt 2 \), \( f \) must be a straight line of slope \( 2 \) on that interval.

steps.explain: The gradient jumps from \( -2 \) to \( 2 \) at \( x=2 \), so \( f \) has a sharp corner (a local minimum) there — the two line pieces must meet at \( x=2 \) to keep \( f \) itself continuous, even though \( f' \) is not.

steps.explain: This gives a V-shaped graph with vertex (minimum) at \( (2,0) \), passing through \( (0,4) \) and \( (4,4) \). Pitfall: drawing a smooth curve at \( x=2 \) — since the gradient jumps discontinuously, the correct sketch has a sharp corner, not a rounded turning point.

questions.stem: What is \(\int \frac{1}{(2x+1)^2}\,dx\)?
questions.hint: Rewrite the denominator as a power, then use the reverse chain rule. The derivative of the inside expression \(2x+1\) is \(2\).

steps.explain: Write the integrand as a negative power. This makes the power rule visible.
The inside expression is \(2x+1\), whose derivative is \(2\). The power rule gives a factor of \(1/2\) to account for that derivative.
Rewrite the negative power as a fraction and simplify.

questions.stem: Differentiate \(y=(x^2+1)^4\). Hence, or otherwise, find \(\int x(x^2+1)^3\,dx\).

parts.stem: Differentiate \(y=(x^2+1)^4\).
parts.hint: Use the chain rule: differentiate the outside fourth power, then multiply by the derivative of the inside \(x^2+1\).

steps.explain: The expression has an outside power and an inside function, so use the chain rule.
Differentiate the inside: \( rac{d}{dx}(x^2+1)=2x\). Multiply the two factors.

parts.stem: Find \(\int x(x^2+1)^3\,dx\).
parts.hint: Notice that the derivative of \(x^2+1\) is \(2x\). The integrand has half of this derivative multiplied by the cube.

steps.explain: Let the inside expression be \(u=x^2+1\). Then \(du=2x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx= rac12du\).
Apply the power rule to \(u^3\): raise the power to \(4\) and divide by \(4\).
Replace \(u\) with \(x^2+1\).

questions.stem: What is \(\int (e^x+e^{3x})\,dx\)?
questions.hint: Integrate each term separately. For \(e^{3x}\), divide by the derivative of its exponent, which is \(3\).

steps.explain: Use the sum rule to integrate the two terms separately.
The antiderivative of \(e^x\) is \(e^x\). For \(e^{3x}\), the inner derivative is \(3\), so divide by \(3\).
Add the two antiderivatives and include one constant of integration.

questions.stem: Find \(\int \frac{x}{4+x^2}\,dx\).
questions.hint: The numerator \(x\) is half the derivative of the denominator \(4+x^2\). Use the logarithm rule for \(\int  rac{u\prime}{u}\,dx\).

steps.explain: Identify the denominator as \(u=4+x^2\). Its derivative is \(u\prime=2x\), so the numerator is half of that derivative.
The integral of \( rac{u\prime}{u}\) is \(\ln|u|\). Here \(4+x^2>0\), so absolute-value bars are unnecessary.

questions.stem: Differentiate \(e^{2x}(2x+1)\). Hence, find \(\int (x+1)e^{2x}\,dx\).

parts.stem: Differentiate \(e^{2x}(2x+1)\).
parts.hint: Use the product rule. Differentiate the exponential factor with the chain rule and differentiate the linear factor.

steps.explain: For a product, use \((uv)\prime=u\prime v+uv\prime\). Here \(u=e^{2x}\) and \(v=2x+1\).
Factor out \(2e^{2x}\), then simplify the bracket.

parts.stem: Find \(\int (x+1)e^{2x}\,dx\).
parts.hint: Use the derivative from the previous part: it is \(4(x+1)e^{2x}\). Scale its antiderivative by \( rac14\).

steps.explain: From the previous result, the derivative of \(e^{2x}(2x+1)\) is \(4(x+1)e^{2x}\). Our integrand is one quarter of this derivative.
Integrate both sides and include the constant of integration.

questions.stem: Which of these is the antiderivative of \(\frac{3x^3-2x^2}{x}\)?
questions.hint: First simplify each term by dividing the numerator by \(x\). Then integrate the resulting powers of \(x\).

steps.explain: Divide each numerator term by \(x\) to simplify the integrand.
Integrate each power separately, increasing the exponent by one and dividing by the new exponent.
Simplify the coefficients.

questions.stem: Which of these is the antiderivative of \(2^x\ln 4\)?
questions.hint: Use \(\int a^x dx= rac{a^x}{\ln a}+C\), then simplify \( rac{\ln4}{\ln2}\).

steps.explain: The factor \(\ln4\) is constant. Use the exponential integration rule for \(2^x\).
Since \(4=2^2\), \(\ln4=2\ln2\). Substitute and simplify.
Therefore the antiderivative is

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to \(\int \tan^2 x\,dx\)?
questions.hint: Use the identity \(	an^2x=\sec^2x-1\), then integrate the two terms.

steps.explain: Rewrite the square using the trigonometric identity \(1+	an^2x=\sec^2x\).
Integrate term by term. The derivative of \(	an x\) is \(\sec^2x\), and the antiderivative of \(-1\) is \(-x\).

questions.stem: Differentiate \((\ln x)^2\). Hence, or otherwise, find \(\int \frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx\).

parts.stem: Differentiate \((\ln x)^2\).
parts.hint: Apply the chain rule: differentiate the square, then multiply by the derivative of \(\ln x\), which is \(1/x\).

steps.explain: Treat this as the chain rule with outside function \(u^2\), where \(u=\ln x\).
Use \( rac{d}{dx}\ln x= rac1x\), then multiply.

parts.stem: Find \(\int \frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx\).
parts.hint: Use the result from part (a): the integrand is half the derivative of \((\ln x)^2\).

steps.explain: Part (a) gives \( rac{d}{dx}(\ln x)^2= rac{2\ln x}{x}\). The integrand is therefore half this derivative.
Integrate and include the constant.

questions.stem: A particle is moving along a straight line. The particle is initially at rest. The acceleration of the particle at time \(t\) seconds is given by \(a=e^{2t}-4\), where \(t\geq0\). Find an expression, in terms of \(t\), for the velocity of the particle.
questions.hint: Velocity is an antiderivative of acceleration. After integrating, use the initial-rest condition \(v(0)=0\) to find the constant.

steps.explain: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, so integrate each term with respect to \(t\).
The particle starts at rest, so at \(t=0\), velocity is zero. Substitute this condition to find \(C\).
Substitute the constant back into the expression for velocity.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function \(y=f(x)\) is given by \(f\prime(x)=3x^2+2x-1\).

parts.stem: Find the \(x\)-values of the two stationary points of \(y=f(x)\), and determine the nature of the stationary points.
options: \(x=-1\) is a maximum and \(x=\frac13\) is a minimum
\(x=-1\) is a minimum and \(x=\frac13\) is a maximum
\(x=1\) is a maximum and \(x=-\frac13\) is a minimum
parts.hint: Set \(f\prime(x)=0\) and factor the quadratic. Use \(f\prime\prime(x)\) to decide maximum or minimum.

steps.explain: Stationary points occur where the first derivative is zero. Factor the quadratic.
Set each factor to zero to find the two stationary \(x\)-values.
Differentiate again: \(f\prime\prime(x)=6x+2\). At \(x=-1\), this is \(-4<0\), so there is a maximum. At \(x= rac13\), it is \(4>0\), so there is a minimum.

parts.stem: The curve passes through the point \((0,4)\). Find an expression for \(f(x)\).
parts.hint: Integrate the given derivative term by term, then use \(f(0)=4\) to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Find \(f(x)\) by integrating each term of \(f\prime(x)\). Include an unknown constant.
Use the point \((0,4)\), which means \(f(0)=4\), to solve for the constant.
Write the function with this value of \(C\).

parts.stem: Hence sketch the curve, clearly indicating the stationary points.
parts.hint: Use the function from part (ii). Mark its two stationary x-values, calculate their y-values, and use the maximum/minimum information from part (i) to shape the curve.

steps.explain: First calculate the coordinates of the stationary points using \(f(x)=x^3+x^2-x+4\).

Use the stationary-point types: the curve has a local maximum at \((-1,5)\) and a local minimum at \((\frac13,\frac{103}{27})\). It also crosses the y-axis at \((0,4)\). Draw a smooth cubic through these points.
steps.work: \(f\prime(x)=3x^2+2x-1\text{ determines the increasing/decreasing shape between the two stationary points.}\)

parts.answer: A correct sketch is a smooth cubic rising to a local maximum at (-1, 5), falling to a local minimum at (1/3, 103/27), then rising again; it passes through (0, 4).

parts.stem: For what values of \(x\) is the curve concave down?
parts.hint: A curve is concave down where its second derivative is negative. Differentiate \(f\prime(x)\) once more and solve the inequality.

steps.explain: Differentiate \(f\prime(x)=3x^2+2x-1\) to obtain the second derivative.
Concave down means \(f\prime\prime(x)<0\). Solve the inequality.

questions.stem: The graph of \(y=f\prime(x)\) is shown. The curve \(y=f(x)\) has a maximum value of \(12\). What is the equation of the curve \(y=f(x)\)?
questions.hint: Read the gradient function from the straight-line graph, integrate it, then use the maximum value to determine the constant.

steps.explain: The graph of \(f\prime(x)\) is a straight line through \((0,4)\) and \((2,0)\). Its slope is \((0-4)/(2-0)=-2\), so \(f\prime(x)=4-2x\).

steps.explain: Integrate the gradient function to obtain the family of curves.
The maximum occurs where the gradient is zero: \(4-2x=0\), so \(x=2\). The maximum value is 12, so substitute \((2,12)\) into the curve to find \(C\).
Substitute \(C=8\) into the equation.

questions.stem: Find \(\int (2x+1)^4\,dx\).
questions.hint: The inside function is \(2x+1\), whose derivative is 2. Apply the reverse chain rule and account for this factor.

steps.explain: The derivative of the inside expression \(2x+1\) is 2, so include a factor of \( rac12\) when reversing the chain rule.
Raise the power by one and divide by the new exponent 5.

questions.stem: The rate at which water flows into a tank is given by \(\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}\), where \(V\) is the volume of water in the tank in litres and \(t\) is the time in seconds. Initially the tank is empty. Find the exact amount of water in the tank after 10 seconds.
questions.hint: Integrate the rate from time 0 to time 10. The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so use a logarithm antiderivative.

steps.explain: Volume gained is the integral of its rate. Use the initial empty condition as the starting volume.
The derivative of \(1+t^2\) is \(2t\), so the antiderivative is \(\ln(1+t^2)\). Substitute the limits.
Give the exact volume with its unit.

questions.stem: Two particles move along the \(x\)-axis. When \(t=0\), particle \(P_1\) is at the origin and moving with velocity \(3\). For \(t\geq0\), particle \(P_1\) has acceleration given by \(a_1=6t+e^{-t}\). When \(t=0\), particle \(P_2\) is also at the origin. For \(t\geq0\), particle \(P_2\) has velocity given by \(v_2=6t+1-e^{-t}\).

parts.stem: Show that the velocity of particle \(P_1\) is given by \(v_1=3t^2+4-e^{-t}\).
parts.hint: Integrate the acceleration to get velocity, then use the initial velocity \(v_1(0)=3\) to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Integrate each term in \(a_1=6t+e^{-t}\).
At \(t=0\), the particle has velocity 3. Substitute these values and solve for \(C\).
Put the constant into the expression for velocity.

parts.stem: When do the two particles have the same velocity?
parts.hint: Set the two velocity formulas equal. The exponential terms cancel, leaving a quadratic equation.

steps.explain: Same velocity means \(v_1=v_2\). Substitute both expressions.
Add \(e^{-t}\) to both sides, then collect terms on one side.
Factor and solve.

parts.answer: For t>0, x1−x2=t(t²−3t+3)>0, so the particles do not meet again.
parts.stem: Show that the two particles do not meet for \(t>0\).
parts.hint: Integrate both velocity functions to find each position, using the fact that both start at the origin. Then factor the difference of the positions and check its sign.

steps.explain: Position is the integral of velocity. Integrate \(v_1=3t^2+4-e^{-t}\) and use \(x_1(0)=0\) to find the constant.
Integrate \(v_2=6t+1-e^{-t}\) and use \(x_2(0)=0\).
Subtract positions. The shared exponential and constant terms cancel.

The quadratic is always positive because its discriminant is negative: \((-3)^2-4(1)(3)=-3<0\), and its leading coefficient is positive. Since \(t>0\), the whole product is positive, so the positions cannot be equal.

questions.stem: A particle is moving along the \(x\)-axis. The graph shows its velocity \(v\) metres per second at time \(t\) seconds. When \(t=0\), the displacement \(x\) is equal to 2 metres. What is the maximum value of the displacement \(x\)?
questions.hint: Displacement increases while velocity is positive, so its maximum occurs where the graph crosses the time axis. Add the area under the velocity graph to the initial displacement.

steps.explain: From the graph, velocity decreases from \(8\,	ext{m/s}\) at \(t=0\) to zero at \(t=4\,	ext{s}\). While \(v>0\), displacement is increasing.

steps.explain: The displacement gained is the triangular area under the velocity graph from 0 to 4 seconds. Its base is 4 seconds and its height is 8 metres per second.
Add the starting displacement of 2 metres. At \(t=4\), velocity becomes zero and then negative, so this is the maximum position.

questions.stem: Find \(\int \frac{x}{x^2-3}\,dx\).
questions.hint: The denominator has derivative \(2x\), which is twice the numerator. Use the logarithm antiderivative rule.

steps.explain: Let \(u=x^2-3\). Then \(du=2x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx= rac12du\).
The antiderivative of \(1/u\) is \(\ln|u|\). Restore \(u=x^2-3\) and include the constant.

questions.stem: In a theme park ride, a chair is released from a height of 110 metres and falls vertically. Magnetic brakes are applied when the velocity of the chair reaches \(-37\) metres per second. The height of the chair at time \(t\) seconds is \(x\) metres. The acceleration of the chair is given by \(\ddot{x}=-10\). At the release point, \(t=0\), \(x=110\) and \(\dot{x}=0\).

parts.stem: Using calculus, show that \(x=-5t^2+110\).
parts.hint: Integrate acceleration twice: first use the initial velocity to find the velocity, then use the initial height to find the position.

steps.explain: Acceleration is the second derivative of height. Integrate \(\ddot{x}=-10\) to find velocity.
At release, \(t=0\) and \(\dot{x}=0\), so solve for \(C_1\).
Integrate velocity to find height.
At release, \(x=110\) when \(t=0\), so \(C_2=110\).

parts.stem: How far has the chair fallen when the magnetic brakes are applied?
parts.hint: First find when the velocity reaches \(-37\,	ext{m/s}\). Substitute that time into the height formula, then subtract the height from 110 m.

steps.explain: From part (i), velocity is \(\dot{x}=-10t\). Set it equal to the brake speed and solve for time.
Substitute \(t=3.7\) into the height equation to find the height at braking.
The chair has fallen from 110 m down to 41.55 m. Subtract to find the distance fallen.

questions.stem: Water is flowing in and out of a rock pool. The volume of water in the pool at time \(t\) hours is \(V\) litres. The rate of change of the volume is given by \(\frac{dV}{dt}=80\sin(0.5\pi t)\). At time \(t=0\), the volume of water in the pool is 1200 litres and is increasing.

parts.stem: After what time does the volume of water first start to decrease?
parts.hint: The volume decreases when its rate of change becomes negative. Find the first positive zero of \(80\sin(0.5\pi t)\) after the initial increase.

steps.explain: The volume stops increasing and starts decreasing when its rate is zero and then changes from positive to negative.
The first zero after \(t=0\) occurs when the angle reaches \(\pi\).

parts.stem: Find the volume of water in the pool when \(t=3\).
parts.hint: Integrate the rate to obtain volume, use \(V(0)=1200\) to find the constant, then substitute \(t=3\).

steps.explain: Integrate the rate. Since the derivative of \(0.5\pi t\) is \(0.5\pi\), the antiderivative includes a factor of \(160/\pi\).
Use the initial volume to find \(C\).
Substitute \(t=3\). As \(\cos(1.5\pi)=0\), the cosine term is zero.

parts.stem: What is the greatest volume of water in the pool?
parts.hint: A maximum occurs when the rate changes from positive to negative. Use the first such time from part (i) in the volume function.

steps.explain: The rate changes from positive to negative at \(t=2\) hours, so the volume is greatest then.
Use \(V(t)=1200+ rac{160}{\pi}[1-\cos(0.5\pi t)]\), found by integrating and applying \(V(0)=1200\).
Since \(\cos\pi=-1\), simplify.

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to \(\int e^{2x}\,dx\)?
questions.hint: The derivative of the exponent \(2x\) is 2, so divide by 2 when integrating the exponential.

steps.explain: Use the reverse chain rule for an exponential with exponent \(2x\). The derivative of the inside is 2.
Check by differentiating the result: the chain rule multiplies by 2, cancelling the factor \( rac12\).

questions.stem: Find \(\int \frac{1}{(x+3)^2}\,dx\).
questions.hint: Rewrite the integrand as \((x+3)^{-2}\) and use the power rule for antiderivatives.

steps.explain: Write the denominator as a negative power.
Raise the power from \(-2\) to \(-1\), divide by \(-1\), and include the constant.

questions.stem: The gradient function of a curve \(y=f(x)\) is given by \(f\prime(x)=4x-5\). The curve passes through the point \((2,3)\). Find the equation of the curve.
questions.hint: Integrate the gradient function to get \(f(x)\), include a constant, then substitute the point \((2,3)\) to find it.

steps.explain: Integrate \(f\prime(x)=4x-5\) term by term and include the constant of integration.
Use the point \((2,3)\), which means \(f(2)=3\), to find \(C\).
Substitute \(C=5\) into the function.

questions.stem: Differentiate \(3+\sin 2x\). Hence, or otherwise, find \(\int\frac{\cos 2x}{3+\sin 2x}\,dx\).

parts.stem: Differentiate \(3+\sin 2x\).
parts.hint: Differentiate the sine using the chain rule: the derivative of the inside angle \(2x\) is 2.

steps.explain: The derivative of the constant 3 is zero. Differentiate \(\sin(2x)\) with the chain rule.

parts.stem: Find \(\int\frac{\cos 2x}{3+\sin 2x}\,dx\).
parts.hint: The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator. Use the logarithm rule for \(u\prime/u\).

steps.explain: From part (i), the derivative of the denominator \(3+\sin2x\) is \(2\cos2x\). So the numerator is half of this derivative.
Integrate using \(\int u\prime/u\,dx=\ln|u|+C\), including the factor \(1/2\).

questions.stem: Find \(\int e^{4x+1}\,dx\).
questions.hint: The exponent has derivative 4. Reverse the chain rule by dividing by 4.

steps.explain: For an exponential, the derivative of the inside exponent becomes a factor. The inside \(4x+1\) has derivative 4.
Check by differentiation: multiplying by 4 cancels the factor \(1/4\).

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(\dot{x}=10-2t\), where \(x\) is the displacement from the origin in metres and \(t\) is the time in seconds. Initially the particle is 5 metres to the right of the origin.

parts.stem: Show that the acceleration of the particle is constant.
parts.hint: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Differentiate \(10-2t\) with respect to time.

steps.explain: Differentiate the velocity function to find acceleration.
The result does not contain \(t\), so it is constant.

parts.stem: Find the time when the particle is at rest.
parts.hint: At rest means the velocity is zero. Set \(10-2t=0\) and solve.

steps.explain: Set the given velocity equal to zero because the particle is at rest.
Solve for \(t\).

parts.stem: Show that the position of the particle after 7 seconds is 26 metres to the right of the origin.
parts.hint: Integrate velocity to get position, use the initial position \(x(0)=5\), then substitute \(t=7\).

steps.explain: Integrate velocity and include an unknown constant.
Initially the particle is 5 m right of the origin, so \(x(0)=5\). Use it to find \(C\).
Substitute 7 seconds.

parts.stem: Find the distance travelled by the particle during the first 7 seconds.
parts.hint: The particle changes direction when velocity becomes zero at \(t=5\). Find the distance for 0–5 s and 5–7 s separately, then add.

steps.explain: The velocity is positive before 5 seconds and negative after 5 seconds, so the particle changes direction at \(t=5\). Position is \(x=10t-t^2+5\).
From 0 to 5 seconds, position changes from 5 m to \(x(5)=50-25+5=30\) m. The distance is 25 m.
From 5 to 7 seconds, position changes from 30 m to 26 m, so the distance for this part is 4 m. Add both distances.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function \(f(x)\) is \(f\prime(x)=4x-3\). The line \(y=5x-7\) is tangent to the graph of \(f(x)\). Find the function \(f(x)\).
questions.hint: At the tangent point the curve and line have the same gradient. Set \(f\prime(x)=5\), then use that point on the line to find the integration constant.

steps.explain: The tangent line has gradient 5. At the point of tangency, the curve gradient equals 5, so solve \(4x-3=5\).
Find the tangent-line y-coordinate at \(x=2\). This point is also on the curve.
Integrate the derivative to find the general form of \(f\).
Use \(f(2)=3\) to solve for \(C\), then state the function.

questions.stem: Find \(\int\frac{4x}{x^2+6}\,dx\).
questions.hint: The denominator derivative is \(2x\), which is half of the numerator. Apply the logarithm rule.

steps.explain: Differentiate the denominator: \( rac{d}{dx}(x^2+6)=2x\). The numerator \(4x\) is twice this derivative.
Integrate using \(\int u\prime/u\,dx=\ln|u|+C\). Since \(x^2+6>0\), the absolute value can be omitted.

questions.stem: Find \(\int\frac{1}{3x^2}\,dx\).
questions.hint: Take the constant \(1/3\) outside the integral and rewrite \(1/x^2\) as \(x^{-2}\).

steps.explain: Rewrite the integrand as a constant times a power.
Use the power rule: increase the exponent from \(-2\) to \(-1\) and divide by \(-1\).

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle is given by \(\dot{x}=1-2\cos t\), where \(x\) is the displacement in metres and \(t\) is the time in seconds. Initially the particle is 3 m to the right of the origin.

parts.stem: Find the initial velocity of the particle.
parts.hint: Substitute \(t=0\) into the given velocity formula and use \(\cos0=1\).

steps.explain: Initial velocity means evaluate the velocity at time zero.

parts.stem: Find the maximum velocity of the particle.
parts.hint: Cosine ranges from \(-1\) to 1. To make \(1-2\cos t\) as large as possible, use the smallest cosine value.

steps.explain: In \(\dot{x}=1-2\cos t\), the velocity is largest when \(\cos t\) is smallest, which is \(-1\).
Substitute \(\cos t=-1\).

parts.stem: Find the displacement \(x\) of the particle in terms of \(t\).
parts.hint: Integrate the velocity to obtain displacement, then use the initial position \(x(0)=3\) to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Displacement is an antiderivative of velocity. Integrate each term.
At \(t=0\), the particle is 3 m right of the origin. Substitute to find \(C\).
Write the displacement function.

parts.stem: Find the position of the particle when it is at rest for the first time.
parts.hint: At rest means \(\dot{x}=0\). Find the first positive solution for \(t\), then substitute it into the displacement formula from part (iii).

steps.explain: Set the velocity to zero and solve for cosine.
The first positive angle with cosine \(1/2\) is \(t= rac\pi3\).
Substitute this time into \(x=t-2\sin t+3\), using \(\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3/2\).

questions.stem: The gradient of a curve is given by \(\frac{dy}{dx}=6x-2\). The curve passes through the point \((-1,4)\). What is the equation of the curve?
questions.hint: Integrate the gradient to find the curve with a constant, then substitute \((-1,4)\) to determine that constant.

steps.explain: Integrate the gradient function.
Substitute the point \((-1,4)\).
Write the equation with this constant.

questions.stem: Differentiate \(y=\sqrt{9-x^2}\) with respect to \(x\). Hence, or otherwise, find \(\int\frac{6x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\,dx\).

parts.stem: Differentiate \(y=\sqrt{9-x^2}\) with respect to \(x\).
parts.hint: Rewrite the square root as a power of \(1/2\), then use the chain rule on \(9-x^2\).

steps.explain: Write the square root as a power and differentiate using the chain rule.
Simplify the factors and rewrite the negative power as a fraction.

parts.stem: Find \(\int\frac{6x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\,dx\).
parts.hint: The integrand is \(-6\) times the derivative found in part (i). Multiply its antiderivative by \(-6\).

steps.explain: Part (i) gives \( rac{d}{dx}\sqrt{9-x^2}=- rac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\). The integrand is \(-6\) times this derivative.
Integrate the derivative and multiply by \(-6\).

questions.stem: A tap releases liquid A into a tank at the rate of \(2+\frac{t^2}{t+1}\) litres per minute, where \(t\) is time in minutes. A second tap releases liquid B into the same tank at the rate of \(1+\frac{1}{t+1}\) litres per minute. The taps are opened at the same time and release the liquids into an empty tank.

parts.stem: Show that the rate of flow of liquid A is greater than the rate of flow of liquid B by \(t\) litres per minute.
parts.hint: Subtract liquid B’s rate from liquid A’s rate and combine the two fractions over the common denominator \(t+1\).

steps.explain: Write the difference between the rates.
Combine the whole-number terms and the fractions.
Cancel the common factor and simplify.

parts.stem: By how many litres is the volume of liquid A greater than the volume of liquid B in the tank when the taps are closed after 4 minutes?
parts.hint: The rate difference from part (i) is \(t\). Integrate this difference from 0 to 4 minutes to get the volume difference.

steps.explain: The volume difference is the integral of the difference in flow rates over the 4 minutes.
Find the antiderivative and substitute the limits.

questions.stem: Find:

parts.stem: Find \(\int\sqrt{5x+1}\,dx\).
parts.hint: Use the reverse chain rule: the inside expression has derivative 5, and the power is \(1/2\).

steps.explain: Write the root as a fractional power.
Increase the power by 1, divide by \(3/2\), and account for the inside derivative 5.

parts.stem: Find \(\int\frac{x}{4+x^2}\,dx\).
parts.hint: The denominator’s derivative is \(2x\), twice the numerator. Use the logarithm integration rule.

steps.explain: The derivative of the denominator \(4+x^2\) is \(2x\), so the numerator is half of this derivative.
Integrate using the logarithm rule.

questions.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by \(\ddot{x}=4\cos2t\), where \(x\) is displacement in metres and \(t\) is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of \(1\text{ m/s}\).

parts.stem: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by \(\dot{x}=2\sin2t+1\).
parts.hint: Integrate acceleration to get velocity. Use the initial velocity at \(t=0\) to find the constant.

steps.explain: Velocity is an antiderivative of acceleration. Integrate, accounting for the inner derivative 2.
At \(t=0\), velocity is 1. Substitute to find \(C\).
State the velocity expression.

parts.stem: Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.
parts.hint: At rest, set the velocity to zero. The first positive angle for which \(\sin(2t)=-1/2\) is in quadrant III.

steps.explain: Set the velocity from part (i) equal to zero.
The first positive angle with sine \(-1/2\) is \(2t= rac{7\pi}{6}\).
Divide by 2 to find the time.

parts.stem: Find the displacement, \(x\), of the particle in terms of \(t\).
parts.hint: Integrate the velocity from part (i), then use the initial position \(x(0)=0\) to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Integrate \(\dot{x}=2\sin2t+1\).
The particle starts at the origin, so \(x(0)=0\). Substitute this condition.
Write the displacement as a function of time.

questions.stem: In the diagram, name all labeled points where the first derivative is positive, \( f'(x) > 0 \).
questions.hint: The first derivative f'(x) is positive where the curve is rising (increasing).

steps.explain: Understand f'(x) > 0
steps.work: \text{The first derivative } f'(x) \text{ represents the gradient of the curve. When } f'(x) > 0 \text{, the curve is sloping upwards (increasing) from left to right.}

steps.explain: Analyze the graph visually
steps.work: \text{Identify the sections of the curve that are going up. This happens between the local minimum B and the local maximum D, and also to the right of the local minimum G.}

steps.explain: Select the correct points
steps.work: \text{Point C is located between B and D. Point H is located after G. Both lie on the upward-sloping sections, so their gradients are positive.}

questions.stem: In the diagram, name all labeled points where the first derivative is negative, \( f'(x) < 0 \).
questions.hint: The first derivative f'(x) is negative where the curve is falling (decreasing).

steps.explain: Understand f'(x) < 0
steps.work: \text{The first derivative } f'(x) < 0 \text{ when the curve is sloping downwards (decreasing) from left to right.}

steps.explain: Analyze the graph visually
steps.work: \text{Identify the sections of the curve that are going down. This happens to the left of turning point B, and between turning points D and G.}

steps.explain: Select the correct points
steps.work: \text{Point A is to the left of B. Points E and F are between D and G. Thus, } f'(x) < 0 \text{ at A, E, F.}

questions.stem: In the diagram, name all labeled points where the first derivative is zero, \( f'(x) = 0 \).
questions.hint: The first derivative is zero at stationary points (turning points).

steps.explain: Understand f'(x) = 0
steps.work: \text{The first derivative } f'(x) = 0 \text{ at stationary points (turning points or horizontal points of inflection).}

steps.explain: Analyze the graph visually
steps.work: \text{Identify the turning points: local minima are at B and G, and a local maximum is at D.}

steps.explain: Select the correct points
steps.work: \text{The stationary points are exactly at B, D, and G.}

questions.stem: In the diagram, name all labeled points where the second derivative is positive, \( f''(x) > 0 \).
questions.hint: The second derivative is positive where the curve is concave up (holds water).

steps.explain: Understand f''(x) > 0
steps.work: \text{The second derivative } f''(x) > 0 \text{ when the curve is concave up (shaped like a cup holding water).}

steps.explain: Analyze the graph visually
steps.work: \text{Identify the concave up regions. The curve is concave up on the far left (before inflection point C) and on the far right (after inflection point F).}

steps.explain: Select the correct points
steps.work: \text{Points A and B are in the left concave up region. Points G and H are in the right concave up region. Thus, A, B, G, H.}

questions.stem: In the diagram, name all labeled points where the second derivative is negative, \( f''(x) < 0 \).
questions.hint: The second derivative is negative where the curve is concave down (spills water).

steps.explain: Understand f''(x) < 0
steps.work: \text{The second derivative } f''(x) < 0 \text{ when the curve is concave down (shaped like an umbrella spilling water).}

steps.explain: Analyze the graph visually
steps.work: \text{Identify the concave down region. The curve is concave down between the two inflection points C and F.}

steps.explain: Select the correct points
steps.work: \text{Points D and E lie between C and F, inside the concave down region. Thus, D, E.}

questions.stem: In the diagram, name all labeled points where the second derivative is zero, \( f''(x) = 0 \).
questions.hint: The second derivative is zero at inflection points where concavity changes.

steps.explain: Understand f''(x) = 0
steps.work: \text{The second derivative } f''(x) = 0 \text{ typically occurs at points of inflection, where the concavity changes from up to down, or down to up.}

steps.explain: Analyze the graph visually
steps.work: \text{Identify where concavity changes. It changes from concave up to down at C, and from down to up at F.}

steps.explain: Select the correct points
steps.work: \text{The points of inflection are C and F.}

questions.stem:
Find the derivative \( f'(x) \) of the function:
\( f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 \)
questions.hint: Differentiate term-by-term using the power rule.

steps.explain: Differentiate each term using the power rule
Simplify the derivative expression

questions.stem: For the function \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 \) with derivative \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 \), determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Evaluate f'(0) and check its sign.

steps.explain: Evaluate the derivative at x = 0
Determine the state based on the sign of the derivative
steps.work: \text{Since } f'(0) = -9 < 0 \text{, the function is decreasing at } x = 0.

questions.stem: For the function \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 \) with derivative \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 \), determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = 4 \).
questions.hint: Substitute x = 4 into f'(x) and check whether it is positive, negative, or zero.

steps.explain: Evaluate the derivative at x = 4
Determine the state based on the sign of the derivative
steps.work: \text{Since } f'(4) = 15 > 0 \text{, the function is increasing at } x = 4.

questions.stem: For the function \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 \) with derivative \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 \), determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = -1 \).
questions.hint: Check the value of f'(-1).

steps.explain: Evaluate the derivative at x = -1
Determine the state based on the value of the derivative
steps.work: \text{Since } f'(-1) = 0 \text{, the function is stationary at } x = -1.

questions.stem: For the function \( f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 \) with derivative \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 \), determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = 3 \).
questions.hint: Find the value of f'(3).

steps.explain: Evaluate the derivative at x = 3
Determine the state based on the value of the derivative
steps.work: \text{Since } f'(3) = 0 \text{, the function is stationary at } x = 3.

questions.stem:
Find the derivative \( f'(x) \) of the function:
\( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 8 \)
questions.hint: Apply the power rule to each term.

steps.explain: Differentiate each term

questions.stem: Find the range of \( x \) for which the function \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 8 \) is increasing. (Write as an inequality, e.g. x > a)
questions.hint: Set f'(x) > 0 and solve for x.

steps.explain: Find the derivative f'(x)
Set the derivative to be strictly positive
Solve the inequality

questions.stem: Find the range of \( x \) for which the function \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 8 \) is decreasing. (Write as an inequality, e.g. x < a)
questions.hint: Set the derivative f'(x) < 0 and solve for x.

steps.explain: Set the derivative to be strictly negative
Solve the inequality

questions.stem: Find the value of \( x \) for which the function \( f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 8 \) is stationary.
questions.hint: Set f'(x) = 0 and solve for x.

steps.explain: Set the derivative to zero
Solve for x

questions.stem: Differentiate \( f(x) = x^4 \), then evaluate \( f'(1) \) to determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = 1 \).
questions.hint: Find f'(x), evaluate it at x = 1, and check if f'(1) is positive, negative, or zero.

steps.explain: Differentiate f(x)
Evaluate f'(1)
Determine the state
steps.work: \text{Since } f'(1) = 4 > 0 \text{, the function is increasing at } x = 1.

questions.stem: Differentiate \( f(x) = (x-2)(x-4) \), then evaluate \( f'(1) \) to determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = 1 \).
questions.hint: Expand f(x) to quadratic form first, find f'(x), and then substitute x = 1.

steps.explain: Expand f(x)
Find f'(x)
Evaluate f'(1)
Determine the state
steps.work: \text{Since } f'(1) = -4 < 0 \text{, the function is decreasing at } x = 1.

questions.stem: Differentiate \( f(x) = (x-1)^4 \), then evaluate \( f'(1) \) to determine whether the function is increasing, decreasing, or stationary at \( x = 1 \).
questions.hint: Use chain rule to differentiate, then substitute x = 1.

steps.explain: Apply the chain rule to differentiate
Evaluate f'(1)

steps.explain: 1. Domain
steps.work: \text{The function } f(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5 \text{ is a polynomial, so the domain is all real } x.

steps.explain: 2. Symmetry
steps.work: f(-x) = (-x)^2 - 4(-x) - 5 = x^2 + 4x - 5. \text{ This is neither } f(x) \text{ nor } -f(x)\text{, so it is neither even nor odd.}

steps.explain: 3. Intercepts and Sign
steps.work: \textbf{y-intercept:} f(0) = -5.\\ \textbf{x-intercepts:} \text{Set } y = 0 \implies x^2 - 4x - 5 = 0 \implies (x-5)(x+1) = 0 \implies x = -1 \text{ or } x = 5.

steps.explain: 4. Asymptotes
steps.work: \text{Since } f(x) \text{ is a polynomial, there are no vertical or horizontal asymptotes. As } x \to \pm\infty, y \to \infty.

steps.explain: 5. The first derivative
steps.work: y' = 2x - 4.\text{ Set } y' = 0 \implies x = 2.\\ \text{When } x=2, y = (2)^2 - 4(2) - 5 = -9. \text{ Stationary point at } (2, -9).\\ y' < 0 \text{ for } x < 2 \text{ (decreasing) and } y' > 0 \text{ for } x > 2 \text{ (increasing). Thus, } (2, -9) \text{ is a local minimum.}

steps.explain: 6. The second derivative
steps.work: y'' = 2.\text{ Since } y'' > 0 \text{ for all } x\text{, the curve is everywhere concave up. There are no points of inflection.}

steps.explain: 7. Any other features
steps.work: \text{The curve is a parabola opening upwards with its vertex at } (2, -9).

steps.explain: 1. Domain
steps.work: \text{The function } f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 \text{ is a polynomial, so the domain is all real } x.

steps.explain: 2. Symmetry
steps.work: f(-x) = -x^3 - 3x^2 + 4. \text{ This is neither even nor odd.}

steps.explain: 3. Intercepts and Sign
steps.work: \textbf{y-intercept:} f(0) = 4.\\ \textbf{x-intercepts:} \text{By testing factors of 4, } f(-1) = -1 - 3 + 4 = 0. \text{ Thus, } (x+1) \text{ is a factor.}\\ x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 = (x+1)(x^2 - 4x + 4) = (x+1)(x-2)^2.\text{ Intercepts at } x = -1 \text{ and } x = 2.

steps.explain: 4. Asymptotes
steps.work: \text{No asymptotes. As } x \to \infty, y \to \infty. \text{ As } x \to -\infty, y \to -\infty.

steps.explain: 5. The first derivative
steps.work: y' = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2).\text{ Set } y' = 0 \implies x = 0 \text{ or } x = 2.\\ \text{When } x=0, y=4. \text{ When } x=2, y=0. \text{ Stationary points at } (0, 4) \text{ and } (2, 0).\\ \text{Using a table of slopes: } (0, 4) \text{ is a local maximum and } (2, 0) \text{ is a local minimum.}

steps.explain: 6. The second derivative
steps.work: y'' = 6x - 6 = 6(x - 1).\text{ Set } y'' = 0 \implies x = 1.\\ \text{When } x=1, y=2. \text{ The concavity changes from down } (y'' < 0) \text{ to up } (y'' > 0) \text{ at } x=1\text{, so } (1, 2) \text{ is a point of inflection.}

steps.explain: 7. Any other features
steps.work: \text{The } x\text{-intercept at } x=2 \text{ is also a stationary point, confirming it is a double root.}

questions.stem: The curve \( y = ax^2 + bx + 5 \) has a turning point at \( (-2, 1) \). Find the value of the coefficient \( a \).

steps.explain: Understand 'turning point'
steps.work: \text{A turning point at } (-2, 1) \text{ gives us two pieces of information: the point lies on the curve, and the derivative is zero at } x = -2.

steps.explain: Use the derivative condition
steps.work: \text{Differentiate the curve: } y' = 2ax + b.\\ \text{Set } y'(-2) = 0 \implies 2a(-2) + b = 0 \implies -4a + b = 0 \implies b = 4a.\\ \text{This is our first equation.}

steps.explain: Use the point condition
steps.work: \text{The point } (-2, 1) \text{ must satisfy the curve's equation. Substitute } x = -2 \text{ and } y = 1:\\ 1 = a(-2)^2 + b(-2) + 5 \implies 1 = 4a - 2b + 5 \implies 4a - 2b = -4.\\ \text{Dividing by 2 gives } 2a - b = -2.\\ \text{This is our second equation.}

steps.explain: Solve the simultaneous equations for a
steps.work: \text{Substitute } b = 4a \text{ from the first equation into the second equation:}\\ 2a - (4a) = -2 \implies -2a = -2 \implies a = 1
